Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their stars' glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

#6623. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

In a food processor, pulse the cream cheese, goat cheese, butter, and garlic powder until the mixture is smooth. Add parsley, chives, and thyme and pulse until well combined. Then season with salt and black pepper.

Transfer the cream cheese mixture to a piece of plastic wrap and gather up the wrap to form a ball. Then transfer the mixture into a large bowl and refrigerate until it’s firm, which should take at least three hours and up to one day.

In a clean food processor, pulse 3/4 cup pecan halves until they are finely chopped.

Roll the cheese ball in nuts and arrange it all on a platter.

Start by cutting a large triangle from a red bell pepper—this will be the face. Next, cut a smaller triangle from a yellow bell pepper for the beak. For the eyes, slice two small rounds from a small carrot. Take a larger carrot and slice it into diagonal ovals to make the feet, then carve little triangles at one end to look like toes. Insert matchstick carrots, pretzel sticks, and mini pretzels into the back of the ball to create the tail. Using the remaining 1/2 cup pecan halves, create wings by overlapping them along each side of the ball. Serve with crackers alongside!

Store leftover cheese ball in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. If possible, remove the pretzels and vegetable decorations before storing, as they can soften over time.

A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

The fossil was so well preserved that researchers identified a cockroach in the stomach that was likely the owl's last meal.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.

"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Mayr, G., Šmídová, L., Richter, A., & Wedmann, S. (2026). Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

#6618. Poulet Basquaise

Rich tomatoes, stewed onions and peppers, and tender bone-in chicken make this Spanish- and French-inspired poulet Basquaise recipe extremely flavorful while still being surprisingly easy to make. Savory and rustic, it’s a stew that’s ideal for making ahead and enjoying all week long. The key ingredient? Piment d’Espelette—the regional spice known for its peppery, smoky essence. If you’re looking to master a classic dish or simply want a reliable, cozy weeknight dinner, then this recipe won’t let you down.

Heat a large skillet with oil and season the chicken with salt. Working in batches, add the chicken pieces and sear until the skin is golden in color, which should take 5 to 7 minutes. Remove the chicken to a heatproof plate.

Then reduce the heat and add the onion, bell peppers, garlic, piment d’Espelette, and salt. You’ll want to stir this once in a while so it doesn’t stick, but also let the vegetables soften. This should take 8 to 10 minutes.

At this point, increase the heat again and add the wine. Scrape up any bits on the bottom and allow those peppers and onions to absorb the wine. The liquid should reduce.

Add the tomatoes and broth and bring to a simmer. Be careful of splattering sauce and adjust the heat as needed. Place the chicken back into the skillet, skin side up, and cook until the chicken is tender and nearly falling off the bone. The sauce should also be thicker and fragrant. This should take about 30 to 40 minutes.

Stir in the chorizo and cook until it’s warmed through. Top it off with thyme and serve!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. It’s certainly a great meal-prep dish. Make this on a Sunday night for lunch Monday and Tuesday.

#6617. Hot Honey Brussels Sprouts

These honey-glazed brussels sprouts are saucy, tangy-sweet, and have a bit of kick. Caramelizing the honey gives it a deeper, toastier sweetness. Vinegar, red pepper flakes, and a good dose of butter transform it into a sticky sauce that seeps into the nooks of each and every sprout. The recipe makes a generous amount: Use it all, or save some for drizzling on pizza a few days later.

The trick to perfectly charred brussels sprouts? Preheat the sheet pan, then arrange the halved sprouts cut side down on the hot metal. It might feel a little fussy flipping each sprout onto its flat side, but the deeply browned results are worth it.

Make the glaze while the sprouts roast or up to five days ahead, then toss everything together just before serving to preserve those crispy edges.

Glossy and pourable, about the consistency of warm maple syrup—not thick like caramel. The honey will foam as it cooks, and the mixture will bubble aggressively when you add the vinegar. Both are normal. The glaze will thicken a bit as it cools, so don’t worry if it seems slightly thin while still bubbling.

They have a noticeable kick, but they’re more tangy-sweet than fiery. The honey and butter temper the chile flakes. If you’re sensitive to spice, use less than the suggested ¾ tsp. or leave the flakes out entirely.

Place a rimmed baking sheet on bottom rack of oven; preheat to 450°. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, and ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large bowl; sprinkle with ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and season with freshly ground black pepper.

Carefully remove baking sheet from oven. Using tongs, arrange brussels sprouts cut-side down on hot baking sheet. Roast brussels on bottom rack until softened and deeply browned, 15–25 minutes.

Meanwhile, bring ¼ cup honey to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook, stirring often, until honey is a deep amber color but not burnt (it will be foamy, that’s okay), 3–4 minutes.

Remove from heat and add ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar (it will bubble up quite aggressively) and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes; whisk until sauce is smooth. Return saucepan to medium heat and add 3 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, whisking constantly, until glaze is glossy, bubbling, and slightly thickened, 3–4 minutes.

Transfer roasted brussels sprouts to a large bowl. Add half the hot honey glaze and scallions and toss to combine. Taste and add more glaze if desired. Transfer to a platter and top with lemon zest. Serve remaining glaze alongside.

Do ahead: Glaze can be made 5 days ahead; refrigerate after cooling.

#6616. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Reeder, H. T et al (2026). Timing of Long COVID Improvement in Prospectively Followed RECOVER-Adult Participants. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/ANNALS-25-05275

#6613. Whole Wheat vs. Sourdough: Which Bread Is Healthier?

How to pick the loaf that fits your life.

Whole wheat bread used to be the gold standard of quick, healthy carbs. Unlike white bread, it uses flour milled from the entire wheat kernel, providing extra fiber and vitamins. But sourdough has exploded in popularity over the past decade, offering a seemingly more natural option made from just sourdough starter, flour, and water. Is this ancient breadmaking method healthier than whole wheat, even if it uses white flour?

As a dietitian, I see this showdown between whole wheat and sourdough all the time. People wonder if the rustic, tangy charm of sourdough beats the wholesome, fiber-packed power of whole wheat. Let’s slice into the details and figure out which loaf deserves a spot on your counter.

Whole wheat is exactly what it sounds like. This bread is made using flour from the entire wheat kernel—the bran, germ, and endosperm. Here’s what that means:

Because it includes all parts of the kernel, 100% whole wheat bread delivers fiber, essential vitamins like folate and niacin, and important minerals such as iron and magnesium. That fiber helps you feel satisfied after eating, supports digestion, and can support blood sugar management and heart health. This combination makes this particular bread a smart, nutrient-dense choice for everyday eating.

It’s a reliable, widely available, research-backed whole grain—and most Americans don’t eat the recommended servings of whole grains every day, which the USDA suggests is more than half of the grains we eat. So, choosing whole-grain bread can help people meet this recommendation.

It seems like everyone and their mother got into baking sourdough a few years ago. We all know it’s delicious, but what makes it special from a health perspective isn't just its ingredients—it’s how it is made.

Sourdough isn’t defined by a specific type of flour. You can make it with all-purpose, rye, or whole-wheat flour; some loaves use enriched/fortified flour for an extra boost of iron and B vitamins. And its magic lies in the fermentation process. Instead of commercial yeast, sourdough relies on a “starter,” which is a living mix of wild yeast and beneficial bacteria (specifically, lactobacilli).

This fermentation process does some pretty amazing things:

In a side-by-side battle, let's see which bread comes out on top:

If your primary goal is to maximize your fiber intake and get a consistent, nutrient-packed loaf, 100% whole wheat is an excellent choice.

If you're looking for a bread that’s easier to digest and offers enhanced mineral absorption, deliciously tangy sourdough is your go-to.

But it is possible to have the best of both worlds. Grab (or bake) a sourdough bread made with 100% whole wheat flour for fiber, nutrient density, and fermentation perks.

Whether you’re Team Sourdough or Team Whole Wheat, there’s one universal truth: your body, and let’s be honest, your soul, will thank you. Because we all know that carbs are good for the soul.

#6611. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6610. Sausage Stuffing Recipe

This sausage stuffing has everything you want on your Thanksgiving plate: crisp, craggy edges, a plush, savory center, and plenty of browned sausage throughout. Torn pieces of country-style bread soak up the broth and eggs without falling apart, turning golden and crunchy on top while staying tender underneath.

Breakfast sausage does much of the heavy lifting. Once browned, its drippings join plenty of butter to cook the onions, celery, and garlic. Fresh sage, parsley, and thyme bring balance, while optional fennel seeds add a little extra aromatic punch.

Uncooked pork breakfast sausage is the first choice. Typically seasoned with sage and black pepper, it brings familiar Thanksgiving flavors and plenty of richness. For some heat, choose spicy breakfast sausage. If you can't find the packaged kind or want to avoid pork, try making your own with our breakfast sausage recipe, using ground dark-meat turkey in place of pork.

This stuffing relies on the fat from breakfast sausage for its flavor. Want a vegetarian version? Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing is a long-standing reader favorite and was the inspiration for this version; use that recipe with vegetable broth for a meat-free stuffing.

What’s the best bread for sausage stuffing?

Look for a sturdy country-style white loaf or sourdough with a relatively thin crust. Avoid soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy, and very crusty artisan loaves, which won’t absorb the broth as readily. Even if your bread is a day or two old, don’t skip drying it in the oven—that’s what helps the stuffing hold its shape.

Can I make sausage stuffing ahead of time?

You can dry the bread a day ahead and store it loosely covered at room temperature. For more ways to get ahead of Thanksgiving, including cooking, refrigerating, and reheating stuffing, see our make-ahead stuffing guide.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Grease a 13x9" baking dish with unsalted butter. Arrange one 1–1¼-lb. loaf country-style white bread, torn into 1" pieces, in a single layer on a large rimmed baking sheet and bake until dried out and golden around the edges, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Meanwhile, melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook 1 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, stirring and breaking into small pieces, until well browned and cooked through, 8–10 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind.

Reduce dial to medium heat and add remaining 8 Tbsp. unsalted butter to fat in pot; heat until melted. Cook 2 medium onions, finely chopped, 6 celery stalks, finely chopped, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. fennel seeds (if using), stirring occasionally, until onions are softened and golden around the edges, 12–15 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth along with sausage, ½ cup (packed) coarsely chopped parsley, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped sage, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped thyme, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Whisk 3 large eggs and remaining 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth in a small bowl to combine, then stir into pot (don’t worry, eggs won’t scramble). Add bread to pot and toss gently to combine. Let sit, tossing occasionally, until liquid is almost completely absorbed, about 10 minutes.

Transfer stuffing to prepared dish (don’t pack or press down) and cover loosely with foil. Place dish on a clean large rimmed baking sheet and bake until stuffing is hot throughout (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°), 35–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 400° and remove foil (no need to remove stuffing from oven while heat increases). Continue to bake until stuffing is light golden brown on top, 25–30 minutes longer.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 1 day ahead; store loosely covered at room temperature. Stuffing can be assembled 1 day ahead; cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before baking.

Editor’s note: This sausage stuffing recipe was first printed in our November 2023 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes →

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

#6606. Apple Fries

Here’s how to make Legoland’s legendary apple fries, complete with the cinnamon sugar coating, caramel drizzle and vanilla whipped cream dip.

Legoland’s most popular food isn’t the usual lacy funnel cake or plate of chicken tenders. Look around for the longest line, and you’ll find it at Granny’s Apple Fries, where deep-fried apple sticks are coated in cinnamon-sugar, drizzled with caramel sauce and served with vanilla whipped cream. Thankfully you don’t need to wait in line (or buy a ticket to the park) to enjoy these legendary apple fries. Here’s how to make a copycat version of Legoland’s apple fries right at home, down to the homemade whipped cream and caramel sauce drizzle.

Peel and core the apples. Using a sharp knife, carefully cut the apples into 1/2-inch sticks.

Place the cornstarch in a large bowl. Add the apple sticks, a few at a time, tossing to thoroughly coat them. Shake off the excess.

In an electric skillet or deep-fat fryer, heat the oil to 375°. Fry the apple fries, a few at a time, until they’re golden brown. Drain the oil from the apple fries by placing them on paper towels.

In a small bowl, stir together the granulated sugar and cinnamon. Immediately sprinkle the mixture over the hot fries. The sooner you sprinkle, the better the mixture sticks.

Editor’s Tip: Never, ever overcrowd your skillet or deep-fat fryer. Doing so may cause a dangerous boil-over. Always work in small batches.

In a small, chilled glass bowl, use chilled beaters to beat the heavy whipping cream until it begins to thicken. Add the confectioners’ sugar and vanilla extract, and beat until soft peaks form.

Serve the apple fries warm with the vanilla whipped cream. If desired, drizzle the apple fries with warmed caramel sauce.

Allow leftover apple fries to cool completely to room temperature, then store them in an airtight container. They can last in the fridge for up to four days.

Yes, you can freeze apple fries. Allow them to cool to room temperature, then transfer them to an airtight container with pieces of parchment or waxed paper between them. Freeze them for up to two months. Reheat them in a 400° oven until they’re crispy and warmed through.

To cut apples for apple fries, peel and core the apples, then cut them into fourths. From there, cut the apple into 1/2-inch slices lengthwise, then turn each slice on its side and cut it in half lengthwise. You should be left with apple matchsticks.

If your apple fries are soggy, the oil temperature was likely too low. When the oil isn’t hot enough, it will soak into the cornstarch and make it soggy rather than crisping the fries. It’s a common deep-frying mistake, so make sure to keep a close watch on the oil’s temperature.

Serve apple fries immediately while they’re still hot. We love to finish them with salted caramel sauce and dip them in the vanilla whipped cream. Serve your apple fries with hot apple cider or homemade hot chocolate to make your treat extra decadent and sweet.

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6603. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6602. I Tried Mashed Potatoes From KFC, Popeyes & Jollibee—There's Only One I'd Order Again

Turns out, a little gravy can make a very big difference.

As a kid who grew up making weekly trips to Boston Market, I’m no stranger to getting mashed potatoes to go. While the chain is a lot harder to find these days, I can still turn to a handful of others when I don’t feel like peeling potatoes and making a batch myself. I might not be rushing to supply my Thanksgiving dinner table with takeout mashed potatoes, but I’m certainly not averse to ordering some to dip my fried chicken into.

I ordered taters from three local fast-food chains to see which one passes muster for texture, seasoning, and all-around flavor. Here’s how it all went down.

Along with Boston Market, I grew up as a regular at KFC. Sadly, its mashed potatoes didn't hit quite as well as I remember. Here, you can order mashed potatoes with or without gravy (the only chain on this list with a gravy-free option), but for this tasting, I opted for the topped version. While they were super creamy, I'd argue they're almost too creamy. They could benefit from a bit more texture and structure. I also found them a bit bland.

I appreciated the gravy, which kept the potatoes from tasting dry, but the potatoes themselves weren't much to write home about.

Popeyes’ mashed potatoes come topped with Cajun gravy, setting them apart from your standard dish. I really enjoyed the flavor of the gravy—it was almost reminiscent of gumbo—and I thought it added a unique element to the mashed potatoes. There was a tiny hint of spice here that also worked really well.

The potatoes are very creamy but thicker than KFC's, and overall, they were more satisfying in terms of both texture and flavor.

Jollibee's taters were quite good and, hands down, the most classic iteration of the bunch. I liked that you could see actual pieces of potato skin in the mashed potatoes. The gravy also tasted the most traditional, with an almost turkey-like flavor. Notably, these were the least creamy potatoes of the three I tried, but thanks to the gravy, they didn't taste dry.

However, the scoop of actual mashed potatoes was pretty meager, and they were drowned in the gravy. Still, I would choose these over the others when I'm looking for that quintessential gravy-and-mashed combo.

#6601. This Is the Jarred Pasta Sauce Ina Garten Always Keeps in Her Pantry

"Store-bought is fine" carries a little more weight when Ina tells you exactly which pasta sauce to buy.

I can happily spend an entire afternoon making dinner. Give me a little music, a glass of wine and something to braise, and I’ll settle in without much concern for when it all reaches the table. It’s a lovely way to cook when I have the time, but leisurely cooking isn’t always practical for busy parents. On most days, dinner needs to fit into my family’s schedule, and my kids don’t want to hear that dinner is still achieving important levels of depth and complexity as it enters its sixth hour on the stove.

But having less time to cook shouldn’t lower our expectations for dinner. A simple plate of pasta can be every bit as satisfying—provided the ingredients involved are worth eating. It’s why I’m particular about store-bought sauce. I’m happy to buy it, but I want to enjoy it as much as anything I spent time making myself.

Ina Garten seems to have arrived at a similar conclusion. Her signature “store-bought is fine” reassurance comes with some excellent recommendations, including the marinara from Rao’s Homemade, a brand I’ve been loyal to for years. It’s a small thing to have in common with Ina, but until I acquire a Parisian apartment of my own, I’ll gladly take it.

“Why make your own marinara when Rao’s marinara sauce tastes homemade?” Ina has said. It’s a reasonable question, particularly coming from someone with very little left to prove in the kitchen.

She’s equally decisive on her website. When a reader asked her favorite jarred marinara, Ina answered, “That’s easy! Rao’s Marinara Sauce.” It also appears among her recommended ingredients in the site’s shopping section.

Her advice to an incoming college student gives the recommendation some practical context. When asked which staples to have on hand, Ina suggested keeping pasta and Rao’s marinara around for a ten-minute dinner. That’s useful advice at any age, particularly once you discover that graduation doesn’t necessarily leave you with more time to cook.

Ina’s comment about homemade flavor gets at why I’ve continued to buy it, too: Rao’s has the richness and depth I want in a sauce, even when I’m serving it with nothing more elaborate than bucatini and Parmesan. I actually look forward to that dinner. The fact that it comes together quickly is just a bonus.

Lately, I’ve been especially impressed with the brand’s new creamy roasted garlic sauce (so much so that I gave it a Taste of Home Award). The mellow roasted garlic and the richness of mascarpone have made it a favorite in my house.

Ina’s explanation of “good ingredients” offers a useful starting point. In Modern Comfort Food, she writes, “They don’t have to be expensive, but they need to be chosen thoughtfully.” Her emphasis is on flavor and choosing ingredients because of what they contribute to the finished dish.

When it comes to Rao’s, she points to slow simmering and good tomatoes, basil, garlic and oregano. That makes the ingredient label a sensible place to begin when comparing jars. The marinara label lists whole peeled Italian tomatoes, followed by olive oil, onions, salt, garlic, basil, black pepper and oregano—and no added sugar.

For a classic marinara, look for that familiar foundation of tomatoes, oil, aromatics and herbs. If you prefer a more savory sauce, keep your eye on the added sugar, too. These are useful details to compare across brands, although the label can only tell you so much about how well the ingredients have been cooked and balanced. In this case, I’m happy to let Ina’s recommendation settle the matter.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6599. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6598. Decorate Your Tree as You Count Down With the Best Ornament Advent Calendars

Usher in the season with a tradition that helps you decorate! The best ornament Advent calendars can be fancy, kid-friendly and even edible.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

As Advent calendars become increasingly popular, the team at Taste of Home continues to hunt for the best of the best. After testing out dozens of Christmas countdowns focusing on tea, chocolate and even booze, we’re pretty much experts in locating the best Advent calendars for every recipient. But there’s one category we particularly love: ornament Advent calendars!

Nothing screams “the holidays” quite like decorating a Christmas tree. And while everyone likes to tackle the job in their own way, mixing it up with a new tradition is such a fun way to make lasting memories. That’s why we love the idea of decorating throughout the season with a new surprise ornament each day.

To help shoppers find the right fit, we’ve listed our favorite ornament Advent calendars below, spanning a range of interests. Happy countdown!

Lenox is best known for its famous spice village. That said, it also offers gorgeous collectibles, most notably porcelain Christmas ornaments. Now, you can enjoy them in an Advent calendar! The Lenox Peanuts ornament Advent calendar is a luxurious keepsake that will last for years to come.

This luxury ornament Advent calendar manifests holiday cheer. Behind each of the 25 doors is a fine porcelain ornament depicting beloved Peanuts characters. Some are detailed snowflakes printed with classic wintery comic-strip scenes, while others are full-figural ornaments featuring fan favorite characters like Snoopy, Charlie Brown, and Peppermint Patty.

Families will build core memories as they unbox each day and add a new ornament to their tree. And because these are built to last for generations, they’re a fun tradition to look forward to year after year. Plus, the pretty gift-ready box makes this ornament set an ultra giftable option for Peanuts fans.

Part artwork, part delicious treats, the 2026 Dandelion Chocolate Advent calendar is a worthy splurge. Recipients enjoy 25 exclusive confections, each handcrafted by one of North America’s most inspired chocolatiers. But that’s not all—each bite is tucked inside an ornament box you can reuse on your tree!

This year’s theme is chocolate inspired by Nordic tales. It also comes with an illustrated storybook with tales adapted from Nordic mythology and folklore, and a gorgeous keepsake star. Plus, enjoy videos for each day featuring Thomas DuBois, an expert in Nordic astral lore, as he shares the mythology behind each day’s tale.

It’s chocolate, so of course it’s going to be delicious. But the flavors certainly make an impression. “So far, this is my favorite chocolate Advent Calendar to date, and I’ve tested quite a few,” raves tester Mary Henn. “The overall experience has been truly exceptional—from the beautifully designed packaging and thoughtful Nordic theme to the incredible variety of chocolates and talented chocolatiers behind them. It’s been a one-of-a-kind experience from start to finish.”

Even want to hang Christmas ham, ornaments and pie on your tree? This googly-eyed ornament Advent calendar is built to manifest giggles! It’s genuinely fun to open up each day and display your new silly ornament on your tree—especially once you read the humorous captions on each.

This calendar sparks so much joy. From the colorful, whimsical details to the funny little quotes and googly eyes, it’s such a cute idea for kids and adults alike. There’s just something about googly eyes that transcends generation! Plus, the ornaments are reusable and sturdy, so you can enjoy them year after year. Because of the excellent quality and fun execution, opening each day feels like celebrating Christmas again and again.

At only $25, it’s incredibly budget-friendly, making it a great white elephant gift.

This Enchanted Forest Christmas ornament countdown includes a dozen 3D ornaments in classic red, green and white hues. Each ornament is ready to hang, thanks to an included ribbon, and comes with a keepsake card., so you can also gift them to your favorite nature lover.

“I’ve tested many FreshCut Paper Advent calendars, and this new version makes a lovely gift,” shares tester Katie Bandurski. “I love that the paper ornaments can be reused year over year, and the animal designs are oh-so sweet. Plus, some Advent calendars have a massive footprint. I love that this sleek set takes up very little space.”

This DIY ornament Advent calendar includes all the bells and whistles for designing their own felt Christmas tree ornaments. While it’s not set up like a traditional calendar—you won’t be opening any doors—the numbered craft kids prove to be exciting enough on their own.

Tester Katie Bandurski tried this Advent calendar and confirms that it’s fun for almost any age, but tots especially will benefit from the easy instructions. Plus—and this is a big one for parents—there’s no mess!

Kids craft 25 ornaments using felt and stickers—no sewing or glue required at all. And while each ornament has its own set of picture instructions, crafters can follow their heart and create something truly unique. The only thing to consider? They might need their own mini Christmas tree to show off their creations!

Our shopping team at Taste of Home consider ourselves Christmas countdown experts. From Advent calendars for women and men to options for kids, we’ve tested hundreds of Advent calendars over the years—and that’s not an exaggeration! This year alone, our team tested more than 80 different options to find the best pick for every kind of recipient. For this piece, we rounded up our favorite ornament Advent calendars available across all the categories we’ve tried.

When shopping for ornament Advent calendars, the primary consideration should be who is unboxing it. For kids, focus on non-breakable options, bonus points for picks that offer an interactive element! For gifting, consider the recipient’s interests. For foodies, an edible ornament Advent calendar is a classic choice. For folks who appreciate the finer things, focus on finding an Advent calendar featuring luxury ornaments made from porcelain.

That depends! For 24-day countdowns, we recommend beginning on December 1. For 12-day calendars, you have the flexibility to start unboxing on day 1, day 12—or you can opt to open a door every other day!

I’ve written and edited content for digital publications, including Taste of Home, Reader’s Digest and Family Handyman. I’m well-versed in curating the internet to help readers find the absolute best buys worthy of their wallet. I’m also one of Taste of Home’s resident Christmas experts. I, along with our team of writers and editors, researched and tested dozens of holiday countdowns across every category to find the absolute best options for 2024, 2025 and 2026.

#6597. Loaded Mashed Potatoes

Mashed potatoes are a classic side dish that can make almost any meal better. They’re creamy, fluffy, and nearly perfect…nearly. When thinking of how to improve on a dish already so close to perfection, I decided to go back to the basics. What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato. With this in mind, I combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. In it, light, airy mashed potatoes are topped with all of the classic baked potato fillings—cheddar cheese, chives, bacon, and sour cream—for a dish that truly embodies the best of both worlds.

The beauty of these potatoes is that they can go with any number of dinners. Serve them alongside your favorite protein—chicken, steak, pork chops, the world is your oyster—or alongside a few lighter sides like any of our green salads, caramelized Brussels sprouts, or roasted green beans.

Any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 to 4 days. If you haven’t already added the toppings, store them separately. Whatever you do, don’t let leftovers go to waste. We’ve got plenty of leftover mashed potato recipes to make sure you get the most out of the special spuds.
