#6524. The 2026 Restaurant Dishes of the Year

From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites

Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.

From a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

When experiencing a five-course tasting menu ($145), I wasn’t expecting toast to be a main attraction. But even with competition from luxurious courses featuring everything from a complex Hokkaido scallop to an assertive charred rib-eye with peaches, All Well’s puffed grain toast left a lasting impression.

After three years at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with Noah Sandoval, fellow Oriole alum and James Beard winner for Best Chef: Great Lakes, to open the ambitious West Loop restaurant All Well, which offers both a la carte bar options and the aforementioned tasting; the toast is only available as part of the latter experience.

The dish arrives to the table amplified with nutty buckwheat butter sweetened with honey, the backdrop for a pasta stuffed with triple-cream Délice de Bourgogne and a cauldron of salty chicken brodo. You’ll dive into the pasta, of course, using the bread to sop up the rich beurre blanc. Like a performer waiting in the wings for their monologue, the puffed grain toast takes center stage. The toast effectively offsets the creaminess and saltiness of the rest of the dish, but can stand on its own even without the accompanying pasta. Its subtle sweetness almost acts as a mid-meal dessert, a distinctive break in a seamless dinner you don’t quite want to end. — Isaiah Reynolds, audience editor

The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. I fully admit this Midwestern-born, California-raised girl doesn’t encounter ruddy callaloo greens as often as she’d like (my hunch is neither do most Oklahomans). No matter. What Black manages to do with this deceiving pile of greenish-brown mush, dank with hand-picked crab and sparkling with curry spices, translates the soul of Caribbean home cooking in a single scoop. I didn’t know it was possible to be overwhelmed by a sense memory from a life that’s not your own, but this heady appetizer does that, served with a side of crisp taro chips and worth lingering over all afternoon with a couple of Red Stripes. — Lesley Suter, brand director

To understand California cuisine in 2026, look no further than Henrietta, a neighborhood bistro that has struck a just-right balance of precision and ingenuity while imbuing a feeling of nostalgia that begs locals and travelers alike to return. The restaurant’s intentions come across most clearly in its roast chicken, served as a just-salty-enough half chicken hunked into handheld pieces with deep, smoky char marks. The prize chicken pile gets tucked onto a plate alongside a scorched lemon half and a heaping, chicory-heavy Caesar panzanella blanketed under a layer of Parmesan that could be a snowcap on a stretch of the San Gabriel Mountains. With the chicken, Henrietta nods to forebears (namely San Francisco’s Zuni), while making the dish its own with a Baja-born Caesar salad that feels distinctly Los Angeles, dotted with torn fistfuls of bread from the neighboring local Clark Street Bakery. Of course, 2026 continues to be the year of the Great Chickening, where roast chicken has become many a restaurant’s calling card — and an easy way into the cultural cache. In Los Angeles alone, Sqirl (with its new dinner menu) and Pasjoli have both put out progressive, near-intoxicating spins on the dish, but Henrietta’s has lodged itself into the collective imagination with its brazen simplicity. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

The striking cantaloupe and verjus terrine at Nashville’s Junior offers a glimpse into the minds of chef Philip Krajeck and chef de cuisine Brian Mejia, the duo behind the high-technique kitchen. A “terrine” slice arrives with pieces of cantaloupe suspended in a clear gelatin made with verjus, the pressed juice of unripened grapes. One corner is covered in tiny, diced cubes of cantaloupe dressed in citrus-forward turmeric oil; another gets draped in chamomile-steeped cream. The mix of textures and flavors comes together in a dynamic symphony: the bright, acidic cubes of summer-ripened fruit against the calming mellowness of chamomile and gelatin layers that meld cantaloupe juice sweetness with crisp verjus.

The dessert’s structural elegance, which highlights a French variety of melon grown by a local farmer, may not immediately reveal its full complexity: Clear gelatin features a layer of clarified cantaloupe juice with encased melon slices, stacked between two layers of verjus gelatin. The melon gets compressed to intensify its flavors. Somehow, Junior managed to make Jell-O cool again — and dare I say, even sophisticated? — an example of Junior’s steady confidence that makes the restaurant an irresistible experience. — Dianne de Guzman, lead editor, Eater SF

Though people outside the Midwest may not be familiar with freshwater whitefish walleye, there it’s a classic comfort food, a staple of Lenten fish fries, state fair booths, and Lake Erie fishermen’s freezer stashes. At Rosy, chef Vinnie Cimino leans on that familiarity to help convince his customers to experience a beloved ingredient in an entirely new way. Pickled walleye cheeks ($17) have been a recurring staple — if a fleeting one — on Rosy’s Eastern European-leaning menu since the restaurant opened in February 2026. Kate’s Fish in Cleveland’s historic West Side Market provides walleye filets for sister restaurant Cordelia; when breaking down and fileting each fish, the fishmongers save the cheeks until they have a formidable stash. About every three weeks, Rosy can offer pickled walleye cheeks for around four days at a time. It’s a thoughtful move for sustainability, but also for succulence, as fish cheeks are a prized cut for their luscious texture.

Cimino conceived the dish as a nod to Jewish fish-pickling practices (for me, the results also brought to mind a tender ceviche). Seasonal vegetables are pickled with lemon — an earlier version invoked German-style potato salad, spring brought asparagus, and, when I went in June, bell pepper, carrot, and dill were in the mix. They’re then combined with the cheeks, which get a separate hot-pickling treatment involving red wine vinegar, salt, sugar, bay leaf, peppercorns, and coriander. “People really gravitate toward it,” Cimino says. “We’ve built up a great trust with our diners.” While the dish won’t be replacing fried walleye at area fish fries anytime soon, Cimino feels proud that when at Rosy, diners have been more than willing to go along with him for the ride. — MF

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6522. Green Bean Casserole

Green bean casserole belongs on every Thanksgiving spread. If you're scrambling to figure out how to perfect the classic side dish, look no further. I ditched the cream of mushroom soup for a homemade cream sauce and fresh sautéed mushrooms, but don’t worry—this dish is still super-simple to make. You only need 8 ingredients and a little over an hour to make it. Keep reading on for my top tips to make this classic side dish the best it can be:

What People Are Saying:"Once you have this, you'll never be able to go back to the Campbell's gray sodium laden sludge & soggy canned green beans recipe! This is amazing! Your whole family will change their minds about green bean casserole." - CyanCarrot

"This is the best green bean casserole I've ever made! It was easy enough that I could read it through twice, and then just make the dish without having to refer to the text of the recipe! It turned out great, my family ate it up! Without using a can of condensed soup, I could control the amount of salt...this made from scratch sauce tastes more mushroomy than a can of condensed soup!" - GreenBike

The very first step is blanching the green beans. This may seem a little fussy, but it's the best way to start cooking the beans to preserve their crispy texture and bright green color as they continue to bake in the oven. It's easy, but just requires a little setup. Cook the beans in salted water for a few minutes, then immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking process. That's it!

On to the aromatics! This is what takes this casserole truly over the top. Cook sliced onions in butter until just starting to soften, anywhere from 7 to 10 minutes.

Add the mushrooms and let everyone get to know each other. Make it even better by adding some garlic; in my opinion, the more, the merrier. Your kitchen will smell amazing. Pour the aromatics into the bowl with the blanched beans.

Time for the sauce. No need to wipe out the pot, just melt a stick of butter, then toast the flour.

Slowly pour in the milk and whisk, letting the sauce come to a simmer, until nicely thickened. Be sure to taste for salt and pepper.

Add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

Some tips: Make sure to let it cool to room temperature before baking, or add a couple of minutes to your timer to adjust to the colder temperature. Whatever you do, DON'T forget to add the fried onions until after the first round of baking. If they're added before refrigerating, they'll get soggy instead of having that signature crispy crunch.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container (or cover your casserole dish with storage wrap) before refrigerating. This side will last up to 4 days refrigerated (look through our Thanksgiving leftovers ideas for some creative inspo for what to do with them), and leftovers can be reheated in the microwave or oven.

#6521. Chatpata Potato Chip Tower

Cookbook author Rachel Gurjar doesn’t usually jump on food trends, but the potato chip tower called to her. “Chips are already great as is, but I knew a version inspired by chana chor—a fiery street snack made from flattened, fried black chickpeas tossed with onions, chiles, lemon, and chaat masala—would kick it up a notch,” she writes in her debut title, East to East. Chatpata is a Hindi word that means salty, sour, spicy, and sweet at the same time, and this chatpata potato chip tower absolutely lives up to its name. While you can use any potato chips you like—or even substitute tortilla chips, pita chips, or fried pita bread—Gurjar recommends thick kettle-cooked chips, as they stay crispy longer.

“This is typically a dish I only make on Thanksgiving, but since I started making it, my very picky 22-year-old daughter has started requesting it for her birthday dinners.”

Baking meatballs and green beans on two sides of the same sheet pan streamlines the cooking process for this saucy, savory dinner.

Cut into little squares for an appetizer, or serve wedges for a vegetarian main or standout side.

This brussels sprout pasta recipe taps nutty brown butter, crunchy pecans, and hot Italian sausage to create an easy dinner bursting with fall flavors.

Treat collards like salad greens with a walnut-speckled dressing.

Plopped on a creamy tomato sauce, these peppers are a repeat-worthy one-dish dinner.

You’ll want to put this creamy (but dairy-free) green sauce on everything and it’s particularly sublime under crispy-skinned salmon.

Spicy, tangy, and a little sweet, it’s our deputy food editor’s go-to marinade.

Tender ground beef, savory pancetta, and a splash of white wine make this slow-simmered Bolognese worth the wait.

Save this three-ingredient marinade for nights when you just can’t.

#6519. The 2026 Best New Bakeries in America

Precision pastries are sweeping the nation. These bakers are leading the charge.

If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game.

Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

If one new place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he launched his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

The bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

Born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

Stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

San Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

Vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

#6518. I Tried Taco Bell’s New FLAMIN’ HOT Menu Items To See If They Really Bring The Heat

One of these could've used a few extra sauce packets.

I'll try just about anything Taco Bell puts on its menu, and whatever I order usually ends up drenched in hot sauce. So when I heard the chain was adding a new FLAMIN' HOT offering (and bringing back a punchy fan favorite), I was curious whether they'd finally give me enough spice to leave those packets alone. I like my food hot enough to get a few beads of sweat forming on my nose, and with a name like FLAMIN' HOT, I don't think that's asking too much.

There were two contenders: the returning FLAMIN' HOT Grilled Cheese Burrito ($5.49), which I'd missed during its first run, and the brand-new FLAMIN' HOT Mini Taco Salad ($2.49). Both feature Fritos FLAMIN' HOT, so I figured I was in for some decent spice. Here's how that worked out.

I love a good taco salad, especially when the bowl itself is edible. But my first impression of this mini version was that it looked like a pretty ordinary Taco Bell salad. And after a few bites, I wasn't finding much to convince me otherwise.

You've got seasoned beef, refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheddar, and Creamy Chipotle sauce tucked into a crispy flour tortilla bowl. Beneath everything was a layer of reddish rice, which Taco Bell says is seasoned with FLAMIN' HOT Fritos. I could definitely see the color, but whatever was making that rice spicy wasn't doing much for my taste buds.

And speaking of Fritos, I'm still trying to figure out where mine went. They're supposed to be in there, but I genuinely couldn't tell whether they'd been included in my particular serving. I would've loved more of the chipotle sauce, too, because the other ingredients seemed to overpower whatever heat was hiding underneath.

The shell itself was fine, although a little bland and greasy. I’m still pro-taco salads, but I just wish the spice had been more noticeable—especially with a name that makes such a big promise.

The returning burrito is stuffed with seasoned beef, spicy rice, crunchy FLAMIN' HOT Fritos, nacho cheese sauce, sour cream, and Creamy Chipotle sauce. And because Taco Bell clearly believes there's no such thing as too much cheese, the entire thing gets a three-cheese blend grilled onto the outside of the tortilla.

I took a pretty substantial first bite, making sure to get into those Fritos and all its FLAMIN’ HOT components. The nacho cheese had that gloriously gooey, movie-theater quality (complimentary), while the rest of the fillings worked together much better than they had in the salad. There's a lot happening inside this thing, and I was enjoying every bit of it.

Most importantly, I could actually taste the heat. There was a satisfying punch of spice, followed by that little tickle at the back of my throat that tells me something's doing its job. I wasn't desperately reaching for a drink, but the burrito had enough kick to make me happy.

I even went back for another bite of the mini taco salad afterward, and it tasted better with the burrito's lingering heat still in my mouth. Who knew it needed a little help from its menu companion?

Ultimately, the burrito is the one I'd order again. The mini taco salad has potential, and for $2.49, I wouldn't be opposed to giving it another shot. But next time, I'm bringing the extra hot sauce packets it should've saved me from needing.

#6517. Goat Kari

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants."

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

"This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she said.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis showed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers said, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz said. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way."

In ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz said, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly."

Tomasto-Cagigao, E., Reindel, M., Isla Cuadrado, J., Lund Valle, M., Kassadjikova, K., Harkins, K., Fehren-Schmitz, L. (2026). A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2625042123

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6515. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in New York City

The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

It felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a new role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

For me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

“How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in New York.

In the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

As I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in New York.

In the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

As I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

#6514. Bob's Chicken Salad and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6513. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503

The Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592

Chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

“You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

In 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

You’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

Be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580

Across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

The Colmado, Bur says, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

In the run-up to the COP31 U.N. climate change conference, scientists have revealed that global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to drop by 0.4% this year, driven by growth in installed wind and solar power capacity, as well as oil price hikes caused by the Iran conflict. But climate goals are still unlikely to be met.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The world's carbon emissions from oil, gas and coal are projected to decrease by 0.4% this year, driven partly by the expansion of solar and wind power capacity and the price increases caused by the Iran conflict, according to a new report.

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget report was published in the journal Earth System Science Data Nov. 10 and is due to be presented at the U.N. Climate Change Conference's COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, this week.

Global carbon emissions have increased steadily since record-keeping began. This year is projected to have a slight decrease in fossil-fuel emissions, but that is partly due to price increases caused by the Iran conflict.

It is the first time annual carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels have fallen since the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. But the overall emissions picture suggests the world is still likely to miss key climate goals.

"It is an encouraging sign that the growth of emissions is slowing and decarbonisation efforts are starting to make a difference," said Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London who wasn't involved in the research. "However, at 0.4%, the projected decline is very small," Rogelj told Live Science in an email.

The report projects 38.2 billion metric tons (42.1 billion U.S. tons) of emissions of the climate-warming greenhouse gas CO2 from fossil fuel sources this year. Greenhouse gases trap heat by absorbing the sun's radiation, and as their concentrations in the atmosphere increase, so do global average temperatures, leading to altered weather patterns and higher sea levels, as well as other major impacts.

The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand

Part of the 0.4% reduction in CO2 emissions is attributable to 40 countries that have cut emissions over the past decade while growing their economies. These include the U.S., Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Japan and about 30 countries in the European Union, the researchers reported.

When it comes to some of the biggest emitters, annual CO2 emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9% in China, 1.3% in the U.S., 1.5% in the European Union and 1% in Japan, but India's annual CO2 emissions are projected to grow by 4.4%.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Carbon emissions are projected to decrease slightly in the U.S., China and the E.U. but to increase in India.

Fossil-fuel-linked CO2 emissions from the rest of the world are projected to decrease by 0.7%, driven mainly by a 1.9% drop in oil emissions. Some of the report authors suggested in an accompanying paper in Nature Climate Change that this is a short-term response to the global supply constraints and increased prices triggered by the Iran conflict.

"The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand," Rogelj said.

While fossil fuel emissions and demand for oil are declining globally, overall demand for energy is actually increasing.

"Based only on the demand for energy, which has grown, we would have expected an increase in fossil CO2 emissions by about 0.8 gigatonnes," said study co-author Judith Hauck, a biogeoscientist at the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research in Germany.

About two-thirds of that increase in demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, showing that clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions, Hauck said. However, the hike in energy prices that resulted from the Iran conflict also decreased demand by 0.4%, she said.

"So only together with the energy crisis did we bring the change in emissions down to negative," Hauck told Live Science, adding that she expects CO2 emissions to rebound if the conflict ends, as they did after the temporary emissions drop caused by the lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The exceptional circumstances that energy markets experienced this year make it clear that the small projected emissions decline is no reason to declare that emissions are now reducing, but there are hopeful signs, Rogelj said.

"Despite my muted enthusiasm about whether these lower emissions for 2026 represent the start of a long-term decline, the analysis shows encouraging signs of deeper long-term structural changes," he said. "But this shift must accelerate to ensure it is not outpaced by energy demand growth."

The report found that clean energy growth isn't yet fast enough to drive a steady decline in global CO2 emissions attributable to fossil fuels. The study authors expect that to happen in the next few years, Hauck said, as long as there is a continued push to deploy solar and wind power, batteries and electric vehicles.

CO2 emissions from fossil fuels are just part of the picture, though. Because of increases in human-caused peat fires, deforestation and forest fires linked to dry El Niño conditions, total global CO2 emissions from all sources this year are projected to increase slightly from 42.8 billion metric tons (47.2 billion U.S. tons) last year to reach a record 43.3 billion metric tons (47.7 billion U.S. tons) this year, according to the report.

This means that the total budget of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming reaches 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels is now just 150 billion metric tons (165 billion U.S. tons) ‪—‬ equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.

Hauck, like many climate scientists, thinks we have already missed our chance to hit the 1.5 C target and could only get back to that level through extensive removal of CO2 from the atmosphere.

"I'm still hopeful for something between 1.5 and 2 C [3.6 F]," Hauck said. "But for 1.5 degrees, we would need to see such a drastic strong drop in emissions. Based on what we've seen in the past years, even with this strong increase in avoided emissions, I don't think we can make that."

To halt global warming from increasing ever further, the world needs to be more ambitious in its planned emissions cuts, said Rogeli. We need to bring annual emissions down to zero to protect future generations from a double whammy of “having to try to transform economies so that they produce less climate pollution, while dealing with the impacts and damages of an increasingly adverse climate system," he said.

Editor's Note: This article was updated on Wednesday, Nov. 11 at 8:45 a.m. E.D.T. to note that the conclusions about the effect of the Iran conflict on fossil fuel emissions came from a Nature Climate Change paper written by some of the report authors.

Chris Simms is a freelance journalist who previously worked at New Scientist for more than 10 years, in roles including chief subeditor and assistant news editor. He was also a senior subeditor at Nature and has a degree in zoology from Queen Mary University of London. In recent years, he has written numerous articles for New Scientist and in 2018 was shortlisted for Best Newcomer at the Association of British Science Writers awards.
