#6502. The Best Nontoxic Cookware Trusted by BA Editors (2026)

If you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity. As you've thought about getting new pans you may have even searched for the best nontoxic cookware without being totally sure what “toxins” they supposedly do not have in them. So what exactly makes cookware “toxic,” and why do these “safe” or “healthy” pans claim to be better?

The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. These chemicals, which repel liquids, have been used in everything from waterproof jackets to nonstick cookware coatings, and after decades of use, the health concerns raised by scientists started to break through to the public more broadly in more recent years.

Whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them. We’ve tested dozens of nonstick and “nontoxic” pans to find the best options to help you keep PFAS out of your cookware. Read on for the lowdown on all things nontoxic cookware.

When companies label their cookware “nontoxic,” it’s a marketing move as much as anything, designed to position it as a safer alternative to traditional nonstick, which is typically coated in a chemical called polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. And to understand why people began to colloquially refer to old nonstick pans as “toxic,” we need a little history of PTFE.

Discovered accidentally in 1938 and trademarked by chemical company DuPont as Teflon in the early 1960s, PTFE was an earthquake in the home cookware market during the second half of the 20th century because it provided consumers with a completely nonstick, no-oil-needed cooking surface. By the turn of the century, Teflon had become ubiquitous, finding its way into a staggering number of American kitchens in the form of PTFE-coated skillets, muffin tins, baking dishes, and more.

PTFE, though, is just one of thousands of a class of chemicals in PFAS family mentioned earlier. Around 1951, DuPont started using another PFAS called PFOA (short for perfluorooctanoic acid) in its Teflon manufacturing process. Over time, it became clear that PFOA could enter the human body by way of gaseous fumes or chipped coatings and have detrimental effects on human health and the environment, including increased risk of certain cancers, birth defects, ulcerative colitis, and thyroid disease. Under mounting pressure from public health and environmental advocacy groups, manufacturers phased out PFOA by 2013.

These days traditional nonstick cookware is made using PFOA-free PTFE (which is also typically free of PFOS, another harmful PFAS). You’ll see it marketed under names like T-fal, Dura-Slide, or hard-anodized aluminum. While PTFE itself is considered less harmful than other PFAS, there is still a broader concern. Thousands of PFAS compounds remain unregulated, and there is ongoing research into the class of chemicals as a whole. A label that says “PFOA- and PFOS-free” does not necessarily mean the product is free of all potentially risky chemicals in the PFAS family.

While not necessarily the first recorded use of the term, the idea of “nontoxic” cookware was largely introduced to consumers when GreenPan released the first PFAS-free ceramic nonstick frying pans in 2007. Since then, “nontoxic cookware” has come to mean “PFAS-free nonstick cookware.” While there’s nothing inherently incorrect about this characterization, it’s important to recognize the degree to which it has become a marketing buzzword.

While “nontoxic cookware” typically refers to ceramic nonstick, which is made from silica using a method called the sol-gel process, any cookware that’s made without the use of harmful chemicals like PFAS can be considered “nontoxic.” That includes some tried-and-true options you probably already know and love: stainless steel, cast iron, and carbon steel.

Ceramic nonstick comes closest to mimicking the ease of traditional Teflon, but like any coating, it will degrade over time and can chip (more on that below). That’s why we recommend getting comfortable with uncoated stainless, cast iron, and carbon steel. With the right technique, your food won’t stick to them either, and they’ll last a lot longer.

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: Yes, but hand-washing recommendedMetal-utensil-safe: Theoretically, but wood or silicone recommendedOven-safe: Up to 600ºFWarranty: 1 year

About ceramic nonstick: I have to be honest here, I've personally sworn off coated nonstick pans for good, because no matter which one you buy, it will only last you a few years tops before the coating starts to degrade and you need to replace it. That said, I understand why people gravitate towards them—and if you're dead-set on buying one, ceramic nonstick is the way to go. These pans are typically made of stainless steel or aluminum and lined with a silica-based coating that makes them nice and slick—for a few years, at least. The exact makeup of that coating varies brand to brand, which is why we’ve spent years testing lots of ceramic nonstick pans to find the ones that best deliver on their nonstick promise.

Our top pick: GreenPan’s ceramic nonstick pans were the first to hit the market in 2007, and the brand’s products have consistently come out on top in our best nonstick pan testing. Its Valencia Pro line is our favorite for a few reasons: It’s hefty enough to feel durable while remaining lightweight enough to be easily maneuverable. It’s also affordable enough that you won’t have to break the bank when you inevitably need to replace it in a few years, and more scratch-resistant than some earlier GreenPan iterations we've tried. Oh, and it's induction compatible too.

A budget option: If you don’t cook on an induction stovetop and are looking for a cheaper option, you can go with GreenPan’s Paris Pro line, which performed similarly to the Valencia in our testing.

Read more about our favorite nonstick pans.

Deeper Carbon Nonstick Frying Pan & Glass Lid

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 1,100ºFWarranty: Lifetime

About carbon nonstick (or nitrided carbon steel): At the outset, these pans act like traditional nonstick but can hold up to high heat, metal utensils, and years of use because they aren’t coated. Instead the carbon steel is nitrided, a process that infuses nitrogen into the metal to make it tougher, slicker, and both corrosion- and rust-resistant.

Our top pick: When we first got a hold of Misen’s Carbon Nonstick pan it seemed like the holy grail for anyone trying to quit Teflon without giving up easy-release eggs. Unlike traditional carbon steel pans, Misen’s version has an aluminum core that heats quickly and evenly, and its surface repels oil straight out of the box. In testing, fried eggs, chicken thighs, and sautéed onions all slid right off with minimal oil (food director Chris Morocco said it was “practically allergic” to eggs). The pan is lightweight and durable and will develop a terrific nonstick seasoning. However, as our lead cookware tester Wilder Davies continued cooking with the Misen, he noticed the initial corn oil seasoning layer started to wear, and the miraculous oil repelling characteristics decreased. Once that happened we assigned four more people, myself included, to work with these pans and we all noticed a reduction in the nonstickiness as time went on. However, the nonstick curve on these has proven to be more U-shaped, as we've continued to cook on and season them, food release started to become easier again.

Read our full review of the Misen Carbon Nonstick Pan.

D3 Stainless 3-ply Bonded Cookware; Saute Pan with lid; 3 quart

D3 Stainless Steel 14-in Skillet with Lid

Available sizes: 10", 12", 14"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime

About stainless steel: Stainless-steel cookware is a staple in home and professional kitchens because of its versatility, durability, and low maintenance needs. Use it on the stovetop, in the oven, or with metal tools—unlike shorter-lived ceramic pans, a stainless-steel skillet can serve you well for a lifetime. And here’s the thing: With the proper technique, stainless steel can release almost as easily as ceramic nonstick. The key in guaranteeing your food slides right off instead of becoming a stuck-on mess is using sufficient fat and heat. Make sure to wait until your oil is shimmering before adding whatever you’re cooking, give it enough time in the pan to let the maillard reaction do its thing, and you should have no issues with stickage.

Our top pick: We’ve tested many types of stainless-steel cookware throughout the years here at BA, and one brand has repeatedly stood out time and time again for its consistently well-made, durable, high-performing products. That brand is All-Clad.

In our testing of stainless-steel frying pans and sauté pans, product testers and Test Kitchen editors alike lauded All-Clad’s D3 Everyday line as the best mix of value and performance for home cooks. The “3” refers to these pans’ 3-ply construction, which features an aluminum core sandwiched between two layers of stainless-steel cladding. That aluminum allows the pan to conduct heat quickly and evenly, and it makes the pan more lightweight than solid stainless-steel cookware. In our testing, we found that those promises held true, and that the D3 pans were easy to clean (just hand-wash with a little soapy water, plus some Bar Keepers Friend if you need a hand getting any remaining bits off) and have continued to perform well over the many years we’ve been using them.

Read more about our favorite stainless steel pans.

D3 3-Ply Stainless-Steel 7-Piece Cookware Set

Includes: 10" fry pan, 3-qt. saucepan with lid, 3-qt. sauté pan with lid, 8-qt. stockpot with lidInduction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime

Our top pick: While we recommend building your lineup of cookware piece-by-piece over time, a preassembled set is a good, fast solution if you’re looking to replace your arsenal of Teflon. This 7-piece collection of top-performing D3 stainless-steel cookware from All-Clad has everything you need and nothing you don’t, making it the best option for most people. Tight on space? This 5-piece version is a great choice too.

Read more about our favorite cookware sets.

Available sizes: 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe up to: UnknownWarranty: Limited lifetime

About cast iron: If you’re willing to put just a bit of work into caring for your cookware, a cast-iron skillet will easily fill the nonstick pan-size hole in your kitchen. Cast-iron cookware will never quite reach the level of nonstick that a Teflon-coated piece offers, but in our testing, we’ve found that a properly seasoned cast-iron pan is on par with ceramic nonstick—plus it only gets more slick over time as you continue to use it.

Our top pick: After testing more than 20 cast-iron skillets over several years, our current top pick is the Lancaster No. 8 because it’s lightweight, it has a smooth pre-seasoned surface that’s nice and slick right out of the box, and it provides even heat distribution. The one downside is that it’s quite pricey compared to something like Lodge’s iconic cast iron, which we recommend as a great budget alternative. The Lodge is probably the pan most people think of when they hear “cast-iron skillet,” and at around $20, depending on where and when you buy it, it’s one of the best values in the cookware world—particularly because you can keep it forever rather than replacing it every few years. In our testing, it performed just as well as many more expensive pans.

Read more about our favorite cast-iron pans.

Available sizes: .425-qt., .85-qt., 1.25-qt., 1.75-qt., 2.75 qt., 4-qt., 5.5-qt., 7-qt., 8.75-qt., 13.25-qt.Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: NoOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About enameled cast iron: You may have also heard of enameled cast iron, which is frequently seen in products like our favorite Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens. Many people expect enameled cast-iron pots and pans to be nonstick because the ones with light-colored interiors sort of resemble the kinds of ceramic nonstick coatings we wrote about above, but in reality, that’s not the case. That doesn’t mean you can’t cook food in these things without it sticking, but you’ll need to use sufficient fat and heat to make that happen, as you do with a stainless-steel pan. The benefit of enameled cast iron is that it provides superior heat retention and distribution, and protects the cast-iron core from rust and acidity. It's become one of my favorite types of cookware to use at home over the past few years.

Our top pick: The Staub Round Cocotte is my personal top pick when it comes to Dutch ovens, and tied with the Le Creuset in our official product testing. I prefer the Staub’s dark textured enamel interior, which is less prone to showing discoloration. In addition to the round cocotte, I also own the braiser and a deep skillet, both of which I find myself pulling out constantly.

Read more about our favorite Dutch ovens.

Available sizes: 8", 10.25", 11", 12.5"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About carbon steel: Carbon steel is sort of the Goldilocks cookware because it affords you the nonstick qualities and lightweight feel of a coated nonstick pan and the durability of a cast-iron or stainless-steel skillet. The one caveat is that in order to achieve those nonstick qualities, you’ll need to spend some time properly seasoning your new pan, just as you would with cast iron. But with a bit of work at the outset and occasional maintenance, you’ll be rewarded with an heirloom-worthy piece of cookware that has a well-earned nonstick patina.

Our top pick: De Buyer is one of those famed, old European cookware brands that lots of American home cooks may not be that familiar with. Its “blue” frying pan comes pre-seasoned and will just get better and better as the seasoning improves. As senior writer Wilder Davies notes, you can take specific steps to season it—use a thin layer of oil (as thin as you can possibly get) and put it in a hot oven for an hour—but you can also just keep cooking with it and that seasoning will develop on its own. Another nice feature of this pan in particular, and one that has nothing to do with its seasoning, is its welded-on handle. That means there are no rivets to clean around when you’re done.

Read more about our favorite carbon steel pans.

What types of kitchen gear is PTFE found in?

A skillet may be the first thing you think of when you think of nonstick cookware, but PTFE coatings show up in a host of other items in the kitchen and beyond. On top of skillets, pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, you'll also find PTFE in rice cookers, waffle irons, baking sheets, and grill baskets.

You may recognize ceramic nonstick as the material of choice of many of the aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-viral cookware companies that started popping up in the late 2010s (I’m looking at you, Our Place and Caraway). Ceramic nonstick pans are made without any PFAS. Instead, a gel made from silica is applied and then dried onto the cookware’s metal body to create a nonstick surface.

Sounds great, right? Well, there are a few caveats, the main one being that ceramic nonstick coatings are not built to last. That means you’ll want to be sure to avoid using metal utensils when cooking with them, opting instead for wood or silicone. You’ll also want to avoid exposing them to extremely high temperatures: Even though ceramic cookware is technically more heat tolerant than cookware made with PTFE, high heat will wear down the pan’s ceramic coating. Many manufacturers claim their pans are oven-safe up to certain (often high) temperatures, but we’d recommend using one of our other recommendations above for any stove-to-oven cooking, as those trips to the oven will only further degrade that ceramic coating over time. Similarly, despite any of being dishwasher-safe, hand-washing your pans will prolong their lifespans.

Even if you treat your ceramic nonstick cookware with the utmost care and attention, you still shouldn’t expect it to last you more than one to three years before it starts to lose its nonstick properties. That’s why the best nontoxic nonstick cookware is not necessarily a coated piece of PFOA- or PFAS-free gear—in fact, we’d argue the best nontoxic “nonstick” pans money can buy are made of cast iron, or carbon steel. While these materials are not actually manufactured or marketed as nonstick, each has nonstick properties that can be achieved with proper use and care. .

The bottom line here is that no one needs a coated pan in their life. There is no recipe on this website (or in this world) that requires you to use one, and we tend to think you’re better off investing some time in learning to cook with a more durable type of cookware than spending you money on a full nonstick cookware set. That said, we’re recommending a range of cookware options here for those who are looking for alternatives to traditional PTFE-base nonstick, including a ceramic option for people who aren’t quite ready to kiss coated nonstick goodbye.

#6500. Mars' Molten Heart is Long Gone, but Some Magma Chambers May Persist

We'll never stop being fascinated by Mars. It's kind of like a failed Earth. It appears as if billions of years ago Mars was warm, wet, and habitable. That ended when its interior cooled and its geodynamo failed.

When its geodynamo failed, its magnetic shield failed. The full force of the Sun bore down on the unfortunate planet, and its warming atmosphere was lost to space.

The loss of atmosphere wasn't the only change. Mars had a powerful volcanic past, and the prominent volcanoes in Tharsis Montes prove that. But the planet is largely believed to have left its volcanic past behind as a consequence of cooling.

But there's growing evidence that the planet isn't totally dormant. Recent evidence from missions like InSight and the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter suggest some ongoing activity. InSight detected more than 1300 Marsquakes, and the Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrochloric acid.

Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a highly corrosive acid with multiple natural sources, including atmospheric ones. The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) collected widespread observations of HCl in Mars' atmosphere at parts-per-billion levels, but initially, it was only detected during perihelion. The HCl detections were attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources driven by greater warmth from the Sun, a naturally-occurring, seasonal pattern.

But new research in Science Advances shows that not all of the TGO's HCl detections can be traced to perihelion. It's titled "Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars." The lead author is Alexander Trokhimovskiy from the Space Research Institute at the Russian Academy of Sciences.

This Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) image shows Alba Mons near the top, with the three Tharsis Montes volcanoes below it, and the massive Olympus Mons to their northwest. Though not as tall as Olympus Mons, Alba Mons is larger by area. The new HCl detections are curiously close to Alba Mons. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/GSFC

The authors acknowledge that Mars is believed to be volcanically dormant, and that Marsquakes and other evidence of more recent volcanic activity is accumulating. However, there's no clear understanding of Mars' modern activity. For instance, many of the InSight lander's detections were attributed to meteorites.

If we were to witness an actual eruption, and the gases that go with it, a new understanding of Mar's interior would arise. But that hasn't happened, and we have to rely on less obvious evidence for Mars' internal state.

"While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl)," the authors write. "Here, we report HCl detections during the cold aphelion season that are isolated in the Alba Mons region." Could these new HCl detections be a window into Mars' interior?

Olympus Mons is known as the largest volcano and the tallest mountain in the Solar System. But Alba Mons is actually the largest volcano by surface area. Like Olympus Mons, it's also in the Tharsis region. (And neither are part of Tharsis Montes, the iconic row of three volcanoes). Alba Mons' volcanic flows reach further than 1300 km from its central summit. One of Alba Mons most significant features is its enormous system of fractures. For multiple reasons, detecting HCl over Alba Mons is intriguing.

"Strongly localized in space and time, aphelion HCl detections, amidst an otherwise absence of HCl at that season on Mars, exhibit marked contrast with prolonged and widespread detections at perihelion," the authors write.

âDetections of HCl at low altitudes, unexplained by observed atmospheric state and models, together with the geological context of the region, hint at an igneous origin of this gas,â Trokhimovskiy et al. write. These most recent HCl directions were in 2025.

This figure show HCl detections by the Trace Gas Orbiter. Blue ones represent perihelion detections, which can be explained by seasonal warming and atmospheric interactions driven by the Sun. Red ones are more enigmatic. They could come from tiny fissures near Alba Mons, almost directly under the detections. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The HCl detections alone may not be enough to oveturn the idea that Mars is dormant. As the authors say, they're just a hint. But there's more. "We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth," the researchers explain.

"These structures have not been identified on Mars in earlier works. For instance, systematic geomorphologic mapping of the northern hemisphere did not consider these landforms," the authors explain.

These panels shows some of the important points in the research. (A) shows Alba Mons and the HCl aphelion detections in yellow. (B) is a CASSIS image from the TGO showing a fractured ridge, while (C) and (D) are HiRISE images from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing smaller fissures the researchers identify as potential HCl sources. (E) and (F) are geological models that can explain HCl is seeping from these fissures. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The researchers calculated the seepage rate necessary to account for the HCl abundance in the aphelion detections. They compared it to the perihelion detections, and included the expected lifetime for HCl to persist in the Martian atmosphere. Their work rules out atmospheric-aerosol interactions as the source for the HCl detected during aphelion. But it also rules out those same interactions for the source of HCl detected during perihelion. That makes sense, since non-seasonal seepage from magma chambers would be happening no matter the season.

"Thus, perihelion HCl is unlikely to be directly volcanic in origin," they write. There could still be a link between igneous HCl and perihelion HCl. "However, a connection between igneous and seasonal HCl may still exist via a mechanism complementary to heterogeneous production," the authors write.

Planets are complicated, as we Earthlings know. Multiple interrelated factors contribute to the whole, and everything changes over time. This work further emphasizes how that's true, even on so-called dormant Mars. "The overall cycle of hydrogen chloride includes irreversible sinks," the authors write, and sinks have to be included in any modelling or understanding of Mars.

"Introducing a volcanic source of HCl, we can propose that a fraction of the perihelion HCl observed in the Martian atmosphere is ultimately of igneous origin," the researchers explain. "Localized igneous sources may therefore act as continuous primary contributors of chlorine, which is subsequently redistributed between atmospheric and surface reservoirs."

But despite the complicated picture of seasonality and surface sinks, their conclusion is clear: "Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior."

Julie Elie, an ethologist at the University of California, Berkeley, tells Live Science's Kenna Hughes-Castleberry about using AI to decode the vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bird calls are far more than pleasant sounds in nature. They are complex forms of communication that can reveal how birds think, learn, cooperate and respond to their surroundings. From intricate songs used to attract mates to alarm calls that warn others of danger, vocalizations offer valuable clues about avian intelligence and social organization.

Julie Elie is an animal behavior researcher and associate project scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She recently won the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for Two-Way Interspecies Communication for her work in studying and deciphering zebra finch communication.

For more than a decade, Elie observed the social behavior of birds, recording thousands of sounds and using machine learning combined with behavioral experiments to decode specific calls.

In this interview, Elie discusses how zebra finches learn and use vocalizations, what their calls reveal about intelligence and social relationships and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to decoding birdsong.

Dr Julie Elie is a computational neuroethologist who studies how social animals communicate. Her research combines behavioral experiments, neuroscience, and computational tools to reveal how animals produce communication sounds, what information they transmit in their vocalizations and how they perceive the meaning of vocalizations.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: What made you study birds and birdsong?

Julie Elie: The beginning of my work with birds dates from my Ph.D. I've always been super interested in animal behavior in general. But I think as a young person, I was more attracted by animals that we relate more easily to, which are mammals, right? Dogs, cats, horses.

I wanted to do a Ph.D. on animal behavior and, more specifically, on relationships between animals. I was interested in how animals interact with each other and what kind of social organization they establish.

[Someone suggested I] work on the zebra finch, and I said, "OK, I've never taken the time to really observe birds very well; might as well start now."

I realized that it's difficult to observe birds because they're not close to you. They can fly wherever they want. When you are out and about in town, in the countryside, and you see birds, they're here, and then they're gone. You don't get to see a lot of their vocal interactions or a lot of their social interactions.

So here I was, studying the zebra finch in cages where they were fully interacting with each other. And the question was, what kind of social organization do they have?

I realized quickly that they were not doing a dominance hierarchy [which was previously thought to be the case], but instead, the most important thing in their life was their partner. They were doing pair bonds, and that's the core of their social organization, [with] males and females pairing for life.

Studying birdsong can help researchers like Elie better understand how the birds navigate their complex environments.

KHC: Why is it important to study birdsong, and what can it teach us about intelligence and behavior?

JE: A level of complexity we were trying to understand was, what are the neural mechanisms that enable those birds to do this process of listening to something and copying it, and reproducing it, and doing a comparison between what they're producing and what they're hearing?

The zebra finch is a just-right middle ground level of cognitive ability that is interesting, where you see this pattern of copying vocalization and producing it. But you can look through the avian kingdom, and some species show more complex behaviors.

We know that there are some species that are able to not only imitate their own vocalizations from their own species, their dad, but they're able to copy other species. So, here in California, for instance, a mockingbird is a bird that is really known to be able to reproduce a bunch of different sounds and is actually incorporating this in their vocalizations.

Parrots are also well known for that because we have them as pets, and they're able to reproduce our own vocalizations as humans. This is kind of crazy, when you think about it, because they don't have the same vocal tract as we do. It's smaller, and they have a different system. I think a high cognitive level is when an animal is able to reproduce a sound that is not in their "native language," let's say, and use it for a goal. We do see this in parrots ‪—‬ they're able to ask you for something or even ask the dog to shut up sometimes, which is interesting. They're able to really use those vocalizations, such as "This is not mine, but I communicate with another species this way."

It shows you how smart they can be, and by studying vocal communication in animals, we are getting a window of what cognitive abilities they have and how the usage reveals their level of smartness.

KHC: Could you walk me through how you ended up decoding bird vocalizations?

JE: I spent countless hours observing zebra finches, and I realized that I could progressively do a match between the social context and the acoustic characteristics of the sound produced. I could recognize these sounds and understand what they "mean."

It's like at home with your cat or dog: Within a couple of months, you figure out every time the cat is doing this kind of sound —‬ "meow" — ‬it means he wants to get out or he's hungry, or he wants to cuddle. Same thing with the dog. It's the same process, but instead of doing this with cats or dogs, I did this with birds and constituted the first acoustic dictionary of zebra finch calls.

However, how do you know you are correct? That you correctly identified the sounds that correspond to the "words" in that species?

Pet owners can often differentiate between different vocalizations in their pets, such as different meowing noises for their cat.

I thought that the best confirmation of whether I was right or not could only come from the zebra finches themselves. Up to now, nobody had found a way to systematically go through the vocal repertoire of an animal and confirm if each identified call type was indeed perceived as a word in that species' language.

To achieve this somewhat impossible discussion with a bird, we designed an operant conditioning experiment where the bird is asked to classify vocalizations that were previously recorded from other zebra finches. The game is simple and relies on two rules. The first one is that every day, only the recordings corresponding to one call type are rewarded by seeds, while the recordings from the other call types in the repertoire are not rewarded. The second rule is that the bird can interrupt recordings and skip to the next one whenever they want, like how you skip through songs on your favorite music app.

The bird is placed in a cage that has a button or a little infrared sensor that it can activate with its beak. Each time it does so, the recording of a vocalization randomly drawn from the library of call types is played. Four out of five times, birds trigger the playback of a call type that will not give them access to seeds. Because they are slightly food deprived, they only really want to listen to the rewarded playback, so they interrupt the nonrewarded calls and only listen for the calls that are going to be rewarded.

Every day, the bird has to find out which call type or "word" is rewarded. They usually figure it out pretty rapidly and then start interrupting the playback of all the other call types. Using this task, we could test a different call type every dayIf they had not been able to do it, it would tell us that the call type we had identified was in fact not existing in their language. If they were able to do it ‪—‬ and spoiler alert, they were! ‪—‬ it meant that we had correctly identified that call type.

The birds told us yes, basically —‬ the organization that you're proposing is correct.

But then we made a surprising discovery. We noticed that birds were making some rare and systematic mistakes. We wondered if these mistakes were coming from the acoustic similarity of the call types — how you might mistake, for instance, the word "glove" for "love" or "hurt" for "heart." Or if they were coming from the semantic similarity of the call types — you could maybe mistake "love" for "heart" if you are remembering about the general meaning of the rewarded word today, which is "love.".

In that last case, it would mean that birds truly have an understanding of their call types' meaning. We found out that birds' errors could be better explained by the meaning [the semantic similarity] of the call types. That is a big discovery in the field of animal communication.

I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird.

KHC: Do you think we are headed toward actually being able to communicate with birds, or do you think it's more that we're still testing the waters and we still need to learn the rest of the language before we get there?

JE: When we say "talking with birds," I think we need to understand that it's not going to be a language. Right now, I am studying the zebra finch; it doesn't mean that I would be able to communicate with a crow once I have a repertoire. So there's this component of when we talk about birds, there are many different species.

I think there's more traction in this particular part of the animal kingdom than in other parts, just because birds are really talkative. Birds use a lot of their vocalizations to communicate with each other. So because of that, I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird, just because they are very talkative.

For now, I found all those words. But we need to understand how those words are [strung] together. So it's not necessarily the case that we need to understand the rules of the dynamic exchanges between individuals or how fast you're responding, but how you are responding and whether that makes sense or not.

They [also] have [body] postures. They have specific displays at the same time they're producing the vocalizations. And if we really want to achieve full communication with another species, we need to get to that level.

It's not tomorrow for sure, it's probably not next year, but I think in the range of 10 years we should get there. Especially with how fast the domains of AI and robotics are. I have some hope that we should be able to get to that point.

KHC: Is there one takeaway you would want our readers to know about your work?

JE: Just one. The most important thing for readers that are not specifically scientists is to realize that, by studying animal behavior more generally, researchers are discovering the intelligence of animals. This is opening our eyes to other species and realizing that we're not the only species that is intelligent on this planet.

This is a lesson to us as another species on this planet, that we are not the only ones that are smart and we need to take this into account in how we are evolving.

We need to realize how we're affecting them and realize that they also have their own internal lives, and maybe we should start to respect them a little bit more.

Editor's note: Some of this interview was conducted via email as part of a follow-up conversation. The interview has been edited lightly for clarity and length.

#6498. The Best Food Gifts Under $100 (That Are Just the Right Amount of Extra)

These luxe but affordable gifts feel sumptuous and whimsical, from eggnog petit fours to a glass ham ornament

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

I take my holiday gift shopping very seriously — if not for my giftee, for my own serotonin-seeking purposes. There’s nothing quite as satisfying as finding the right N/A cocktail bundle for your aunt, or a cake stand that doubles as a chip and dip bowl (the in-laws will love that one) for the avid entertainer.

We’re all on different budgets; some are on the hunt for tasty bargains and piggy-bank-friendly stocking stuffers, while others have a more robust chunk of change set aside for providing big-impact presents You might have already bookmarked Eater’s gift guides that are under-$25, which is full of all kinds of chic home and kitchen goods, but now [turns up gas] we’re shopping at the under-$100 range, which gives us even more wiggle room to sweep your giftees off their feet via a ham-themed ornament, a robust at-home chai kit, or a set of steak knives from Peter Luger.

We’re in prime gift guide season, folks. Fasten your aprons, and let’s shop for every kind of food-loving person on your holiday list.

No cocktail has been living, laughing, and loving harder than the ultra-dirty martini lately. This briny bundle from Big Night brings together the shoppy shop’s sleek olive-themed hors d’oeuvres picks with a jar of Quincy’s big, juicy Castelvetrano olives, Quincy cocktail onions, and bag of Filthy’s cult-fave olive brine.

For my money, a solid indicator of a fun household is whether or not there’s a wild cheese or cutting board in the mix. This psychedelic slab from Fredericks and Mae is both a beautiful serving board and functional chopping block for all of your kitchen needs, because it’s made out of a durable and non-toxic HDPE material.

Fredericks and Mae Red/Blue Cutting Board

The organic Los Angeles lifestyle brand Flamingo Estate has created the pasta-lover’s dream present: a chic trio of pomodoro rosso sauce, angel trumpet pasta, and a bottle of Flamingo Estate’s heritage EVOO. As with the rest of the Estate’s bundles, this set comes housed in one of its signature, ornate green boxes.

Imagine the flex of sawing through a Porterhouse at home with Peter Luger logo-stamped blades, which are made with stainless steel and wood handles that will transport their giftee back to the hallowed halls of the world-famous Brooklyn steakhouse. If you have a bit more room left in your gift budget, I suggest pairing it with some New York strip steaks from Snake River Farms.

Diaspora Spice Co. is one of Eater’s favorite places to buy spices online, because it’s home to dozens of single-origin heirloom spices from (mostly) India and Sri Lanka. As founder Sana Javeri Kadri explains on its site, a core tenant of Diaspora Spice Co.’s operations is rooted in undoing colonialist inequity in the spice trade; in her words: “We’re proud to pay our farm partners an average of 6x above the commodity price. In a system where fair trade is a mere 15 percent premium, we pay what we believe to be a living wage.” The equitable spice brand has partnered with the North Carolina-based pottery and lifestyle brand East Fork on this at-home chai bundle, which features the former’s brand new masala chai blend, Madhur jaggery, a stainless steel strainer, and a panna cotta colorway kuhlad from the indie pottery company.

Eater’s deputy brand director Nat Belkov introduced me to Craighill, a company that reimagines everyday carry and home essentials (think, scissors and carabiners) with a little more design flair. The Brooklyn-based studio redesigned the common wine key, and Belkov tells me that it mitigates all the annoying little things that can go wrong while using a wine opener. “I love the perfect angle on the foil cutter,” he says, “[and] I love that they tapped the knowledge of sommelier André Hueston Mack to make sure it worked well enough to be trusted by members of the industry. Seldom do I run into a product where I genuinely have a hard time choosing between different color variations like here, with the sleek matte black, pop of orange, or classy tortoise finish. But most of all, I love that this thing is guaranteed to work for life.”

MoMA Design Store Bodum Neon Nesting Mixing Bowls (Set of 4)

As a person who drinks coffee every day (and feels horrified when I run out), I would be thrilled to receive this American Girl doll-sized bag (weighing 4 pounds) of beans from the award-winning Joshua Tree Coffee. This year, the Big Bag — which is filled with the beans of your choice — even comes with a cute enamel mug.

Joshua Tree Coffee Big Bag & Bellied Enamel Mug Bundle

The Chitose is kind of like the Ferrari of kettles, because it boils water extremely fast and is made out of professional-grade, scratch-resistant 18-8 stainless steel. Plus, it cuts a cute silhouette and is compatible with induction top stoves.

Japanese Taste Chitose Induction Compatible Japanese Stainless Steel Kettle

These pastel eggnog petit fours come from the acclaimed Los Angeles-based confectionary Valerie Confections, and are made of a rich spiced buttercake, with bourbon ganache layers dipped in white chocolate and garnished with 23-karat gold leaf and chocolate biscuit pearls.

Ghia’s apéritif box is one of those drink-themed holiday gifts that sells out every year, because it pairs the brand’s signature amaro-esque N/A ambrosia with chic glassware from French-American glass artist and designer Sophie Lou Jacobsen. Whether you’re shopping for someone who doesn’t drink or is just trying to drink less alcohol in the new year, it’s a fashionable foot forward in the world of booze-free drinks.

Owning a double burner griddle is the culinary equivalent to flexing a California king size bed, because it can handle all of the pancakes, eggs, and grilled cheese orders from the family (without having to hop between skillets like a stove DJ). We love this one from Lodge, known for its excellent cast iron cookware.

#6497. What You Need to Know About Japanese Knives

The popularity of Japanese knives in home and commercial kitchens has exploded in the last few years, and for good reason: A lot of them outperform their Western counterparts in kitchen tests. Western-style knives are bulkier, all-purpose kitchen tools—years ago, it would be common for many chefs to use the heavy bolster near the heel of the blade to crack open a can of tomatoes during service. Japanese knives (and Japanese-style knives produced by manufacturers elsewhere) are designed with precision cuts in mind and usually have a specific purpose. However, because they’re designed with that specificity in mind, it can be tricky to know what you need and what you’ll use.

Thankfully, we’ve reviewed a wide variety of Japanese-style knives for Bon Appétit and have assembled a roundup to help you identify exactly what your kitchen needs. While there are more styles of Japanese knives than those listed here, these options have all been thoroughly tested, giving us the confidence to speak to each knife’s utility. Before we jump into specific styles, however, it’s useful to give a quick rundown on some of the broad strokes of what makes a Japanese-style knife unique.

Many Japanese knives are designed for push cuts or pull-through slicing rather than the rocking chop of a heavy Western chef’s knife. They tend to have a straighter edge than their Western counterparts, making them slightly less adept at speeding through a mince of herbs, but more precise in their cuts. Most Japanese-style knives also feature a sheep’s-foot tip that curves down to the point, giving the user more control over fine-point work.

Japanese knives are often made with a harder steel than their Western counterparts. Harder steel helps a knife’s edge retain sharpness, which lets manufacturers use steeper sharpening angles for a finer edge. This helps most Japanese knives slice more delicately than Western knives, though harder steel can chip on material like ice or bone.

Traditional Japanese-style knives are only sharpened on one side, giving them a much finer edge than the 50/50 bevel of Western-style knives that are sharpened on both sides. Some modern Japanese knife makers have pivoted to a 50/50 style bevel for ease of sharpening; however, when you’re shopping, you’ll encounter plenty of knives with 70/30 bevel with the inside edge (the left edge for a right-handed knife) sharpened at a steeper angle. A 70/30 bevel is easier to maintain than a single-bevel but offers a sharper edge than a 50/50 bevel.

Many traditional Japanese kitchen knives feature a wa-style handle—an octagonal wood handle that envelops a hidden knife tang (the metal part of the knife that connects to the handle). Wa-style handles help keep knives lighter and nimbler, while many Western-style knives use full-tang construction, adding weight and heft to the blade. Many modern Japanese knife makers, though, combine full-tang knife handles with Japanese blade shapes to create a hybrid-style knife that’s both durable and adept at slicing.

The gyuto, or Japanese chef’s knife, originated in Japan in the early 1900s, when French cooking began to gain popularity in a rapidly modernizing country. This knife style took cues from the traditional French chef’s knife and combined them with elements of traditional Japanese knife making. The resulting Japanese take on a chef’s knife was primarily designed for slicing meat, though it also features a curved edge that makes it easy to chop herbs. Compared to a Western chef’s knife, the gyuto has a straighter blade and a drop point tip with a lower overall profile. This is primarily designed so that the user can place the knife’s tip on the cutting board and draw it through food, taking advantage of the gyuto’s sharp edge and thin blade for precision slicing. But while the gyuto excels at slicing meat, its general shape makes it an overall great pick to anchor your knife collection, and many home cooks opt for a gyuto as their daily driver over a traditional chef’s knife.

We’ve long been fans of the gyuto fan here at Bon Appétit, with MAC’s Professional Hollow Ground Chef’s Knife topping our chef’s knife review for years. For a wicked sharp, more traditional option, we really like the Kazan Arare by Shibata gyuto, which impressed us so much we had to give it its own review.

Increasingly common as a part of brands’ knife sets, the santoku knife is a relatively modern knife shape, first appearing in the 1940s or so. Nicknamed the three virtues knife, the santoku draws on the gyuto, nakiri, and deba to create a well-rounded utility knife that’s great for cutting meat, fish, and vegetables. Typically, these knives feature a pretty steep sheep’s-foot tip for precision point work, a tall heel for push cuts, and just enough curve for pull-through slicing and rock-chopping. A santoku knife is great for well-rounded utility work—think cutting cheese and an apple for a snack, slicing leftover roasted chicken to make a sandwich, or dicing an onion for a curry.

Typically, we like a santoku knife that’s between six and seven inches, so it contrasts with the longer gyuto. Our favorite overall model is the MAC Professional Santoku Knife, but if you’d like a razor-sharp version with a traditional wa-style handle, we love the Kazan Ginsan Nashiji Santoku.

Nakiri knives have a straight edge and a sturdy spine, specifically designed for chopping vegetables. Sometimes referred to as a vegetable cleaver, the nakiri excels at push cuts, making it great for both matchsticking carrots and breaking down tough-skinned squash. Since most gyutos feature thin blades and fine edges, the nakiri also holds a spot in the Japanese knife lineup as a tougher, heavier knife for more demanding tasks. Traditional nakiri knives may also feature a blunt, rounded tip, which can be rotated against the cutting board to create a smooth, chopping motion.

The Tojiro DP Damascus Nakiri is by far our overall favorite tested nakiri knife for its extremely sharp edge and overall balance, but it’s also pricey. We also really like the Tojiro Classic nakiri, though it can have stock issues due to its popularity and price point.

The deba knife is a traditional Japanese knife designed for fish butchery. Unlike a Western fillet knife, which is designed to be flexible and nimble, the deba is a heavy, sturdy blade with a thick spine that gives the heel of the blade a cleaver-like feel. But a deba knife is also designed for precision slicing, and it usually features a traditional single-bevel edge. That single-bevel edge allows the knife to come to a finer point than a double-bevel edge, and the sheep’s-foot tip adds to the deba knife’s ability to portion out delicate fish fillets as well.

We haven’t tested deba knives because they require a bit of knowledge and skill to use them for breaking down whole fish, but if you’re intrigued by the shape and want a cleaver-like knife for your kitchen, the Seki Mago Roku Deba from Kai is an affordable, solid option. Otherwise, we think most people would be better served looking to a nakiri or santoku knife.

Named for the French word petite, which means small, the petty knife is often a replica of the gyuto, just in a much, much smaller form. Most petty knives are around five inches long and feature a thin, lightly curved blade with a drop point tip and heel just tall enough to keep your fingers from bashing into the cutting board. Petty knives are great utility knives for small tasks, like dicing a shallot, slicing garlic, or slicing herbs, but they’re also long and nimble enough to be great slicers. Unless you do a lot of handheld turning and peeling, a petty knife is a great replacement for a paring knife in your lineup.

We found that both the MAC Professional Petty Knife and the Tojiro Classic Petty Knife were sharp enough to slice a steak while still being the perfect size to slice strawberries for your morning yogurt bowl.

Traditionally a fisherman’s knife used for all sorts of purposes on the boat, the funayuki is an old-school knife shape that predates the gyuto and santoku, and it likely helped inspire both shapes. The traditional funayuki is a shorter knife, around seven inches long, with a narrow, pointed tip and a tall heel. They are santoku-sized but gyuto-shaped. Unlike the deba knife, which was a heavy, single-bevel knife used for fish butchery, the funayuki was designed to be light and nimble so that fishermen could fillet their lunch while at sea. These days, most home cooks might pick up a funayuki as a secondary, shorter gyuto, or opt for this shape over a santoku as an all-purpose utility knife with a narrower tip.

Though it’s not as common in modern kitchens, one of our favorite Japanese chef’s knives is the Akiru-Saku Funayuki Gyuto, which is more traditionally shaped like a funayuki but is advertised as a gyuto since the two shapes are so similar.

The kiritsuke is a Japanese slicing knife with an angular “sword tip” that allows the user to make precision cuts. The initial design combined a long slicing shape and tall heel, making the kiritsuke a hybrid knife, similar to the santoku. For most people, the kiritsuke will be a version of an all-purpose chef’s knife that could take the place of a gyuto as a daily driver, with the big difference coming in the shape of the tip.

When reviewing chef’s knives, we found that the Shun Classic Kiritsuke was a great all-purpose chef’s knife with a unique tip that some people might prefer over a gyuto, since it curves upward more like a Western chef’s knife and allows for more of a rock chop motion.

Boning and fillet knives are often unitaskers that don’t see much use unless you’re a fan of home butchery, but the Japanese honesuki is an even more specialized boning knife shape. Designed specifically for poultry, the honesuki is a steep, wedge-shaped knife with a very fine point and a tall heel. The goal is to have a knife that’s delicate enough to slip between a chicken joint while being sturdy enough to cut through cartilage. While the honesuki was designed for a specific purpose, we find that this shape is more versatile and can be swapped in for a petty knife for other small chopping and dicing tasks in ways that a curved fillet knife can’t.

We like the MAC Professional Honesuki as a great option that could tackle most boning-knife tasks while remaining sharp and versatile enough for utility work. If you find yourself breaking down a whole chicken while also wanting a strawberry-slicing knife, the honesuki could be a nonconventional multitasker.

#6496. Using Vibrations and AI, Future Robotic Missions Could Handle Buried Rocks Autonomously

Knowing a planet's surface and subsurface structure is vital when planning robotic and crewed missions to explore it. Before landers, rovers, or crew modules reach the surface, astronauts and mission controllers need to know what they will be landing on. For rovers with a limited energy budget, it's also crucial that they can determine how far rough, rocky terrain extends beneath the surface. That way, they won't waste time and energy trying to clear obstacles they can't possibly move.

In short, scientists and astronauts need to know what's on a planet's surface (and beneath it) before they attempt to land there and conduct science operations. Thanks to a team from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Virginia Tech), scientists could soon have a new set of tools that will allow robotic missions to make these determinations autonomously. These AI-powered tools measure vibrations in surface terrain to determine what lies beneath and how deep structures extend.

The study was led by Yiyan Ruan, a Ph.D. candidate at Virginia Tech, and Erik Komendera, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering (and Ruan's advisor) who once worked as a researcher at NASA's Langley Research Center. The paper detailing their findings was published in IEEE Sensors Journal. The tools they have developed could have profound applications for both space exploration and life on Earth.

View generated from the digital terrain model and the nadir and color channels of the High Resolution Stereo Camera on ESA's Mars Express. Credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin

As they indicate in their paper, estimating the burial depth of partially embedded rocks is a key capability for energy-limited robotic excavation. When obstacles like rock formations are in the way, mission teams need to know how deep the rock extends so they can decide whether to remove the obstacle or avoid it. Ruan and Komendera's solution leverages AI to interpret vibrational data, allowing robots to make those decisions autonomously. As Komendera said in a Virginia Tech press release:

For as long as humans have built things on Earth, we have had to deal with large and heavy obstacles that cannot simply be ignored or scooped out of the way without careful planning. It's easy enough for us to just look at rocks and make some quick, testable judgments. Is this rock resting or partially buried? Can I move this alone or do I need help and tools? But what if robots need to do this? How can robots make those judgments? Now we have an answer.

To test their approach, their team buried 18 concrete blocks of different shapes and sizes in sand at different depths. They then struck the exposed portions of the blocks with an instrumented hammer and remotely measured the vibrations using a device known as a Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV). The results were then input into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), a type of neural network that learns to identify complex, non-linear patterns from data.

Their MLP mapped 11 measurable features to identify the relationship between impulse excitation, exposed rock geometry, and burial depth. Given the range of factors to consider, the task was rather complex. But by teaching their AI to account for them, Ruan and Komendera created models that could reliably determine the blocks' depth.

When the future rovers set down on Mars, they could determine rock depth and obstacle clearance autonomously. Credit: NASA/JPL

"Estimating how deep a rock is buried using vibrations can be tricky," said Ruan. "The feedback is affected by the rock's geometry and the way the soil holds it. By carefully selecting features from vibration measurements and exposed geometry, we were able to produce reliable data using a compact neural network with just two hidden layers."

These models could help robotic missions excavate subsurface rocks, caches of water ice, and remove obstacles along their travel routes. In the meantime, the team plans to keep building datasets and testing their approach for applications on Earth, such as analyzing construction sites and natural disasters to locate where potentially hazardous materials are buried. They could also be used to study unstable rock formations and underground caverns, assisting with resource and construction planning, and advancing exploration of Earth's subsurface.

Further Reading: Virginia Tech, IEEE Sensors Journal

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

#6494. Tiny Solar Whirlpools May Hold the Secret to the Sun’s Blistering Corona

For the second time in a few weeks, weâre writing about research into the temperature gap between the Sunâs surface and its corona. More and more data from various missions continue to feed this wave of discovery. A new paper by Katariina Nykyri of Embry-Riddle, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds to this growing body of work. She argues that millions of tiny whirlpools scattered across the Sunâs surface could be the energetic engine driving that temperature difference.

Earlier this year, the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), located atop HaleakalÄ on Maui, took extremely high resolution images of the Sunâs surface. For the first time, scientists could make out whirlpools of plasma, a few dozen kilometers across, dotted around the Sunâs surface. When this research was published in August, Dr. Nykyri had a bit of a âEureka!â moment, according to a press release from the University.

Her research had focused on Kelvin-Helmholtz waves. On Earth, these are most commonly seen in broken ocean swells or ripple-pattern clouds. However, they are also present elsewhere in the solar system, driving gas patterns on Jupiter. On the Sun, they occur when fast-moving plasma passes slower, magnetized plasma. They contain an absurd amount of mechanical energy. The vortices created by these waves are the very structures DKIST resolved on our starâs surface. As these vortices churn across the solar surface, their vast kinetic energy transfers into the Sun's magnetic fields, converting mechanical motion into magnetic stress.

Fraser talks about the features of the Sun that we are only now getting a glimpse of thanks to new technologies.

Dr. Nykyri set out to answer how much energy these vortices carry and whether it equals the total energy needed to heat the corona. After accounting for the velocity shear, density difference, and vertical heights of the tornadoes, she reached a conclusion. On average, each vortex contains around two septillion ergsâa unit of energy commonly used in solar physics. Across the Sunâs 1.4-million-kilometer surface, millions of these vortices spin up and dissipate every few minutes.

When these vortices dissipate, their energy must go somewhere. According to Dr. Nykyri, it appears to enter the corona through magnetic reconnection. Solar physicists have long thought this process plays a key role in coronal heating. As each KH vortex spins, it squeezes nearby magnetic field lines together. This forms ultra-thin current lines ranging from a few centimeters to meters across.

Once theyâre squeezed past a certain point, they start to violently snap and rearrange. That is the process of magnetic reconnection, and it converts the stored magnetic energy into heat and high-speed plasma jets that are fundamental components of the solar corona. In other words, the KH vortices are the driving force behind the process of reconnection of the Sunâs magnetic field lines.

Frase talks about how hot the Sun actually is.

When the energy they store is released, it has to have somewhere to go, though. And these vortices donât always cause reconnections only in the corona - they also do so on the surface. So why does the corona seem so much hotter? Particle density.

When a magnetic line snaps on the surface, the energy is immediately distributed between trillions of neutral atoms. Each atomâs temperature is commensurately raised, but only by a tiny amount. In the corona, though, atoms are much less plentiful, but the same amount of energy is released. So each magnetic snap increases the temperature of an individual atom by much more in the corona than down on the surface.

According to the paper, only five to eight percent of the mechanical energy stored in the vortices needs to make the journey upward to the corona to replenish the heat that is otherwise radiated away. Even in darker âcoronal holesâ, a max of 21% of the energy from the vortices would be capable of maintaining the temperature of the corona.

This work is a major step toward understanding the heating process, but more research is needed. Scientists still must track wave transmission and polarization through the chromosphere. This will confirm whether as much energy reaches the Sunâs chromosphere as Dr. Nykyri suggests is necessary to maintain coronal temperatures. If her theory holds, some of the high temperatures on our star will be proven to stem from relatively small plasma tornadoes floating across its surface.

#6493. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.
