Testing the Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra was an exercise in both delight and frustration. There’s no disputing its print quality, especially when I produced beautifully detailed game miniatures. But I ran into regular obstacles on the path to those beautiful prints, in the form of poor or even confusing documentation. In a review focusing on ease of use, those pain points really stood out.

Resin printers like the Mars 5 Ultra are especially popular with gamers, who print miniatures for tabletop games. These small figures tend to be packed with details, and printers like the Mars 5 Ultra can generate layers as thin as 0.01 mm, 10 to 20 times thinner than a typical FDM printer. If you want sharp visual details, resin printing is the way to go. The Mars 5 Ultra is an especially good way to learn about printing with resin, thanks to a pair of features that make it more user-friendly than its peers.

First and foremost, it has a tilt-release resin vat that reduces the suction forces between the build plate and the vat. When the build plate bed lifts up after each layer is complete, the vat tilts, creating an angle that makes it easier to separate. (Think of it like pulling off a sticker or a bandage -- it takes far less force if you start on one corner.) Since the tilt-release makes separation easier, your settings don't have to be dialed in quite so precisely in order to get a clean separation from the vat, and support points can be slightly smaller. As a result, you spend less time adjusting settings or removing support marks, and more time enjoying your finished prints.

It also has a very helpful error detection feature, which is great for new printers. If the Mars 5 Ultra detects foreign objects in the vat—usually chunks of supports or models that have fallen off the print plate—it will pause operation and send a notification. That can minimize damage to the model you’re printing, and prevents debris from getting trapped, which could also crack the vat itself. (In general, I think any feature that keeps toxic resin where it belongs is a big value-add.) Both the vat and error detection save time and reduce the frustration of a failed print. They’re also more commonly found on printers that cost twice as much as the Mars 5 Ultra.

Unfortunately, the standout design is somewhat undercut by Elegoo’s confusing and contradictory support documentation. The instructions told me to install Chitubox (an industry-standard slicer) from the included USB stick. But the only slicer on the USB was Elegoo’s SatelLite slicer. Now, I actually like SatelLite, but it’s not what they told me to expect. What’s especially frustrating is that Elegoo actually has a fantastic unboxing video with a clear, easy to follow walkthrough. But there’s no mention of it in the manual and no QR code linking to it on the packaging. So I only saw it when I stumbled across it online.

Setup aside, this is an excellent printer. It’s well designed and easy to use, and produces quality prints with minimal fuss. (Or at least minimal fuss for resin.) The touchscreen is easy to read and well laid out, with an easy to understand user interface. It is a little small, but it’s sensitive enough that I didn’t need to tap twice, even while wearing gloves.

I also love Elegoo’s optional in-box heater. I picked one up when the temperatures plummeted. Since I’d set up the printer in my garage, I thought I’d fall behind on testing. But the heater installed easily and worked spectacularly well. Before I knew it, I was churning out prints even though the weather was well below freezing. But that heater was the reason I was able to get a full test run on the printer, even during a polar vortex.

The Bambu X2D costs about $100 more than the P2S, and for that additional cost it delivers active heating, better venting, and a dual-nozzle design, letting you print more demanding materials faster and with less waste.

Most enclosed printers depend on passive heating, maintaining the internal temperature simply with the captured heat from the nozzle and print bed. By contrast, the X2D has a built-in heater allowing the internal chamber to reach temperatures up to 149 degrees Fahrenheit (65 degrees Celsius). The X2D’s active heating also allows this temperature to be consistent, making it much easier to reliably print materials like Nylon and ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene).

If you want to print material that can withstand the heat of an engine bay or exposure to the elements, the X2D is a fantastic choice. In addition to the active heating, it has an external carbon and HEPA filter to reduce fumes and airborne particles. It also has a dual-nozzle design that reduces waste when printing two-color models, and allows for easy support printing and removal.

The downside to the X2D is that I found it’s surprisingly prone to minor issues and inconveniences. I ran into a weird error when printing the Benchy model that shipped on the internal memory, and had to do additional tweaking to align models and the prime tower on the print bed. None of these would be unusual from another manufacturer, but Bambu has made a name for themselves by delivering the smoothest possible user experience. The X2D doesn’t quite live up to that standard.

It’s a very good printer for both standard and high-temperature filaments. And for the relatively small step up in price, it compares favorably to the P2S if you want to move beyond decorative items and start creating durable objects that can withstand a real-world environment.

There are two types of 3D printer built with home users in mind: FDM and resin. (While other types of 3D printers are available, they’re intended for industrial use, with a learning curve and price tag to match.) As a rule of thumb, FDM printers are faster and produce more rugged prints than resin, while resin printers excel at fine detail.

Fused deposition modeling printers (FDM) are like a hot glue gun for plastic. They feed a strand of plastic filament through a heated metal nozzle, laying out the print onto a heated metal bed. They’re cleaner and easier to use than resin, and require less safety precautions. They tend to have larger print volumes, but they don’t produce prints that are as highly detailed as resin.

Resin printers, on the other hand, create layers of material by dipping a flat bed into a vat of liquid resin, then curing a layer of material with UV light. (It’s similar to the process of making candles, where you dip a wick into wax repeatedly.) They are typically more complicated to use, as the models have to be washed and cured after printing is complete. Printer resins are toxic until cured, and using resin printers requires significant safety precautions. Resin printers produce highly detailed prints, prized by users ranging from tabletop gamers making miniatures to the dental offices, creating surgical implants and guides.

Both types of printing have their pros and cons, depending on your space, your style, and what items you want to print. Generally speaking, FMD printers are good for larger items, items that need to be more durable, or when you need to turn around prints quickly. They are also a good choice if you’ll be printing in areas with less ventilation or if you’ll have children or pets around while printing. Resin printers are a better choice if you want outstanding detail, and have room to set up a cleaning station for your prints.

FDM printers are usually described by the head movement (either CoreXY or bed-slinger) and whether or not it’s enclosed or open frame. CoreXY printers move the head left to right, and front to back. On a bed-slinger, the head moves left to right, but front to back adjustments are made by moving (“slinging”) the bed itself.

Enclosed printers are just that–enclosed on all sides. These are typically CoreXY printers, and allow for higher temperatures and provide filtered vents for filaments that produce more fumes. They also usually cost more than open-bed printers.

To start printing, you’ll need some 3D models and software (called a slicer) to send them to your printer. Luckily, some of the best options are free.

Every 3D Printer uses some type of slicer software, which allows your printer to analyze objects and create a blueprint for making a 3D printed copy. True to its name, it creates a digital model and “slices” it into anywhere from one to a few thousand printable layers, creating the building blocks of a 3D print design. The result is a detailed set of instructions for printing, called G-code. When you load a design, your printer follows the G-code to assemble the design, layer by pre-sliced layer.

Printer manufacturers provide a proprietary slicer or an open-source slicer customized for their specific machines. For testing purposes, I used the slicer provided by the manufacturer. Honestly, once you get used to one slicer, they’ll all feel pretty similar.

Creating your own print designs isn’t necessary, though, if you don’t feel compelled. There’s no shortage of sites with free or paid 3D print designs that you can download and print. Once you have a little bit of experience printing, there’s a whole world of printable tools and products to explore within the 3D printing community.

When a plastic part breaks, there’s a good chance someone else has run into the same issue and created a 3D version of that part to download and print. Many printer manufacturers support some kind of community site, where users can upload, remix, and review 3D models.

Yes, when used properly. Both FDM and resin printers pose safety risks during operation. FDM printer risks include the hot end of an FDM nozzle and fumes from melted plastic. Resin printers pose more risks, as resin itself is toxic, and should not be allowed to touch unprotected skin, and should only be used in an area where the fumes can be safely vented outdoors. Resin printers also use UV light to cure the prints, which can damage your eyes if not properly filtered.

FDM safety precautions are fairly straightforward. First, don’t stick your hand in the print area while the printer is running. This may sound obvious, but it’s surprisingly tempting to do, since sooner or later you’ll spot a bit of loose filament or some other bit of debris laying on the bed in the middle of a print. It’s very easy to reach in and grab that debris without pausing the print -- but the print head moves very fast and without warning. That nozzle is probably around 300 degrees celsius / 580 Fahrenheit, and having it slam into your knuckle can leave a puncture and a burn.

Second, make sure the room where you operate the printer is well ventilated. Proper ventilation is especially important when using high VOC filaments. These include acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and acrylonitrile styrene acrylate (ASA), but the fumes will vary by manufacturer, so err on the side of caution.

Resin requires more extensive safety precautions. You’ll need to invest in PPE such as nitrile gloves, a respirator (use filters rated for VOCs and not just dust debris), and possibly UV safety glasses. When resin printing, venting is even more important. In most cases it’s easy to safely vent your 3D printer, but if you’re concerned, consider getting an air quality monitor to ensure that you’re working in a safe environment.

Your primary expense using a 3D printer is your printing material, which will be plastic filament for these printers, but could be other materials with more advanced models. You can buy a one-kilogram reel of PLA filament for about $12 to $19. If you need a specialty filament, you’ll likely pay double that amount, and prices can go much higher for premium materials.

Then there’s the hit to your electric bill. FDM printers typically use about 50 to 100 watts to operate, depending on what material you’re printing and the ambient temperature. If your electricity is 20 cents per kilowatt-hour, your printers will likely cost less than 2 cents per hour to operate.

Lastly, there will be other costs over time: You may need replacement bed plates for FDM printers, or post-processing supplies for resin printers. Other parts may break and need replacing, as well.

Once you have a print and some compatible printing material, all you need to do is figure out what and how to print. I recommend new printer users pick up some calipers ($30 or so, but you can get away with a $10 set). You can actually 3D print most of the other tools you’ll use. In fact, printing storage bins and organizers for your printing tools is a great way to learn the ropes while making useful prints.

A former residential remodeler and maintenance manager, Dan Stout has worked in nearly every part of the construction and DIY industry, from project planning and permitting to plumbing, drywall, carpentry, and more. He loves to write about the weird history of everyday objects, and to help readers make informed decisions about their homes.

Prior to joining Hearst, he was a video game and technology critic for over 10 years, with bylines at IGN, Gamespot, Variety, Lifehacker, Kotaku, GamesRadar, Flavorwire and Digital Trends, among others. Now, he’s a jack of all trades, helping reviewers share everything they know about all kinds of technical gear, from snowblowers, to running shoes and bicycles, and every kind of gadget imaginable.

#6479. Highly Specific Observations While Scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards

The great dishes, gorgeous restaurants, and quirky cocktails that commanded our attention, even if they didn’t make the big list

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The past year has been one of “Great Chickenings” and fine dining flips, British food invasions and restaurants whose dining rooms feel like living rooms, vibrant global steakhouses and unserious Y2K food. Among the slate of our 2026 Eater Award winners — which also brought undeniable new chef talent, core-memory-forming dishes, and groundbreaking bakeries and bars — are the places we could not stop thinking about for highly specific reasons. While this crop of restaurants and bars did not make the ultimate cut for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, they commanded enough attention during our expansive scouting and research months to deserve acknowledgment. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Cabbage is having its moment. From a star turn on the Sandy Liang runway as a ruffled bag to a hand-painted Bordallo Pinheiro dinner set and a declaration from Vogue that the leafy green has gone “chic,” the cruciferous vegetable is 2026’s “it” girl. The cult of the cabbage has made its way to Monte’s in Montecito, a cozy Korean American bistro where cone cabbage gets coal-roasted and kissed with salty smoked shiitake XO, an umami-heavy spin on the Hong Kong-born sauce. The fall-apart-tender cabbage beds on creamy tofu puree, the whole thing studded with hazelnuts that bring out the vegetable’s innate sweetness. Preparations like the one at Monte’s make it feel as though cabbage isn’t just this year’s distinguished vegetable — its dominance is here to stay. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

Maybe it was the Negroni, the Old Fashioned, and the gingery mezcal-laced Missed Opportunity. Perhaps it was the jetlag (who can say for sure?), but the bathroom at Bobo — the Filipino bar attached to Muhajir in Chicago’s Lincoln Park — left a lasting impression on me. In a world that’s fully embraced the bathroom selfie, Bobo has answered the call with refractory horizontal-mirrored panel walls and colored light that shifts from reds to greens, turning this lavatory into a mesmerizing disco ball. It’s a fitting touch that matches chef Jacob Dela Cruz’s vision for a red-light district-esque tropical hideaway. — Brenna Houck, Eater editorial manager

In a world of outrageous martinis, the one at Greenpoint Malaysian restaurant Kelang earns its playful name. The Dirty Fish riffs on a Vesper with gin, vodka, dry vermouth, and, saliently, fish sauce, which levels up the drink’s savoriness in every way. The pungent condiment mimics olive brine, delivering a salty taste of the sea to the already strong drink, which then gets garnished with wavy scallions and a long sliver of aromatic ginger. The cocktail showcases owner Chris Low’s background as a Malaysian kid who grew up in New York. It’s simply presented — a cloudy drink in a stemmed coupe glass with those gloating garnishes — and pairs best with that fluffy paratha served over creamy and spicy dal. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

Gone may be the days of business power lunches at Wolfgang Puck’s Spago or Grill on the Alley that required a suit and tie. In their place, a new arrangement has emerged — the low-key power lunch. There may be no better place for the midday meal masquerading as a meeting right now than at Little Fish in Melrose Hill, the first full-service restaurant from the former pop-up-turned-fish sandwich window. The light-filled dining room hums during daytime with flexibly scheduled creatives and well-dressed parents toting young children, all adults in the room sipping wine picked by sommelier Kae Whalen. On the menu, a tuna melt from maverick chefs and owners Anna Sonenshein and Niki Vahle will convert even nonbelievers, especially when paired with peppery fries dunked in horseradish aioli. Of course, there is the calling card fried fish sandwich, but smarter diners go for the beach sandwich layered with guindilla peppers and soy-cured mussels and a bay leaf chip stracciatella flecked with chocolate chips. Melrose Hill and its confluence of independent restaurants has morphed into a miniature walkable neighborhood — the perfect place to see and be seen. And what’s more low-key power lunch than that? — RR

Historically, California is a gold mine of kitsch restaurants, from Clifton’s Republic to the pillowy pink dining room at the Madonna Inn. Night Hawk is the next jewel in that camp crown; the Greek-influenced San Diego restaurant is an anchor of Coronado Island’s hypermaximalist new Baby Grand hotel and beckons diners into a lush, faux-rock-filled outdoor dining room with pink clamshell chairs, waterfalls, and cocktails that have names like the Adonis in Bloom and Spanakopita Punch. In short: Tony Duquette by way of an acid tab. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

British food hit a fever pitch nationally this year as Americans awakened to the allure of meat pies and mushy peas. But if any restaurant truly dispelled notions of the country’s cuisine as dull or bland, it was Ambassadors Clubhouse, with its extensive menu of Punjabi showstoppers such as seven-layer, aloo-filed, Amritsari-style samosas; butter chicken in the form of lollipop-like chops with a heady char; and matka Beliram lamb, its crimson oil heralding intense flavor. In opulent, velvet-adorned surroundings that feel like a hideaway from the city, this luxe London import deliciously makes the case that Indian food is as essential to British cuisine as fish and chips. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

The most beautiful new restaurant in California is tucked into a shopping center in Montecito’s tony upper village. Little Mountain, which opened in November 2025 under chef Diego Moya, gives more to the scene than just a locavore menu that leans into live-fire cooking — it brings a bona fide, Architectural Digest-worthy destination that I would get married (and remarried) in. It may be hard to decide which room to sit in should you land a reservation in time: the comfortable dining room with gold-veil natural lighting and plush caramel booths and banquettes; the larger-party table that foregrounds an open kitchen and its centerpiece hearth; the dim, dark bar that may be the sexiest sliver of drinking den on the Central Coast; the covered patio that leads into a monarchial private dining area; or the outdoor patio that evokes dining in a home garden. Anywhere you sit, you can’t go wrong, especially as the food starts landing in front of you. — NF

Chef Theo Adley opened Heretík last spring, and it has brought a breath of fresh, San Sebastián-esque sea breeze air into the Denver dining scene. The French- and Basque-leaning restaurant serves an endless summer menu of dishes like Santa Barbara uni, a playful pan con tomate martini, and scallops à la plancha with bearnaise and seaweed. The menu’s coastal Euro allure gets amplified by its interior design choices, which sprinkle in vintage furniture and tapered, wax drip-laden candles — but with a name like Heretík, you know that all of that romance is going to come with a healthy dose of cheek. — FK

Chickens, you can’t take credit for this one: The British-inspired pub Dean’s proved that bigger is not always better with its take on a Scotch egg, which employs quail eggs instead of the typical chicken ones. In larger Scotch eggs, what appears in each bite can be inconsistent. But the result of the shrunken-down approach here is a reliably favorable ratio of meat to egg, in which each bite at once encompasses crunchy breading, tender meat filling, runny yolk, and just enough still-bouncy egg white. It’s as nonnegotiable at Dean’s as a pint of Guinness. — BM

Ladyfish in Portland, Maine, has been clear about one thing since the beginning: “A summer fling,” the restaurant declared when it announced its May 2026 arrival. Jordan and Marisa Rubin of Portland sushi spot Mr. Tuna convinced chef Christine Lau to relocate from New York City to helm the seasonal seafood pop-up. Lau, whose resume includes Japanese-Italian and Chino Latino restaurants, brings her distinctive flair to classic Maine ingredients for dishes like scallops in a blanket with fried milk bread and the showstopping twin lobster mountain served with fries, rice cakes, and dan dan au poivre sauce. True to its word, the restaurant closed at the end of October. Here’s hoping the return of next year’s summertime crowds also brings back this match made in seafood heaven. — Stephanie Wu, editor in chief

Los Angeles-born chef Ray Garcia opened Broken Spanish Comedor in Culver City in late 2025, years after his groundbreaking Mexican fine dining restaurant, Broken Spanish, and more casual B.S. Taqueria closed in Downtown Los Angeles. Garcia’s contribution to Alta California cuisine, rooted in Mexican cooking told through a California lens, remains one of the most distinct of this generation of restaurants. Still, he manages to surprise both longtime fans and newcomers to his work: The Comedor, whose name nods to the Indigenous homestyle restaurant tradition in Mexico, feels fresh in its A-frame home. It’s not uncommon for locals and those working in Los Angeles hospitality to stop in for a meal of crispy, crown-whorled chicharron or quesillo-threaded refried lentils; a classics-leaning drinks menu (cócteles, cervezas, vino) keeps the room humming happily. In a year brimming with big restaurant comebacks (see also: Venice’s resurrected Tasting Kitchen and Keith Corbin’s reframed Alta Adams), it feels good to have an Angeleno chef like Ray Garcia capture our collective imagination again. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

If ever there was a destination in need of effective hangover cures, it’s New Orleans. While I was totally ready to rally after a two-bar, two-restaurant evening the night before (I am, of course, a professional), I also wasn’t mad about consuming something fortifying at Casimiro, the charming all-day cafe from award-winning Acamaya chef Ana Castro, the next morning. The restaurant delivered: textbook chilaquiles, impossibly fluffy conchas, crispy pescaditos, and one of the best tortas I’ve ever had. If hair of the dog is in your future in the City That Always Drinks, go with the well-balanced Cynar daiquiri to finish. — Missy Frederick, dining editorial director

The weirdest thing I ate on a pastry this year was “lettuce cream” lacquered onto the BLT Danish at Dahlia in Minneapolis. The chartreuse-colored cream anchored a slice of late-August tomato and dollops of bacon jam atop persistently crisp laminated dough. One bite was enough to make me think, This should be more of a thing. You wouldn’t know at first glance that this bakery, tucked into an office complex, turns out treats of this caliber: jam-filled croissants with speculoos crumble, unassumingly perfect English muffins, plush milk bread and fluffy focaccia for sandwiches. This kind of out-of-the-box baking makes eating pastries right now so fun. — BM

#6478. Popular Weight-Loss Drugs May Have a Surprising Effect on Your Brain

Popular weight-loss drugs may offer benefits that extend beyond metabolism, potentially helping preserve memory and other cognitive abilities.

Medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes may also influence memory and other cognitive abilities. But whether drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide can actually protect the brain remains uncertain, particularly after major clinical trials failed to demonstrate a benefit in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease.

In Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE+ trials, semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer’s progression, even though it produced changes in several biological markers associated with the disease. Researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen have now examined the broader evidence in a review published in Science, exploring whether these medications could still help preserve cognitive function in other groups of patients.

GLP-1 medications influence biological processes involved in both metabolism and brain function. Animal experiments suggest they can affect learning and memory, but studies involving humans have produced inconsistent results. Analyses of patient health records have linked GLP-1 treatment to a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes, although these observational findings cannot establish that the drugs directly provide protection.

The potential benefits may differ depending on the cause of cognitive difficulties. People with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience problems with attention, planning, and mental processing speed. These difficulties are frequently associated with metabolic disturbances and poor vascular health, raising the possibility that treatments targeting these underlying problems could help maintain cognitive abilities.

Stina Börchers, the review’s first author and a researcher affiliated with both universities, believes that identifying the right patients and treatment timing will be essential.

“We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit,” says Stina Börchers.

A central unanswered question is whether any cognitive benefits arise from direct effects on the brain, improvements in metabolic health, or both. Better regulation of blood sugar and other metabolic processes could indirectly support brain function, while GLP-1 signaling may also influence neural processes more directly. Separating these mechanisms could help researchers determine which effects are most relevant to preserving cognition.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review’s senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity medications to investigate these connections.

“Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function,” says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that measure memory and other cognitive abilities from the beginning of treatment. Such studies could help establish whether these medications preserve cognitive function, which patients are most likely to benefit, and whether starting treatment before cognitive difficulties appear makes a difference.

They also caution that potential benefits must be weighed against risks in older or frail patients. Rapid weight loss and declining muscle mass can reduce physical functioning, potentially limiting the overall advantages of treatment. Future studies will need to account for these effects when assessing whether obesity medications can support long-term brain health.

Reference: “Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition” by Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg and Christoffer Clemmensen, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aek9987

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

Fiona Jackson is a freelance writer and editor primarily covering science and technology. She has worked as a reporter on the science desk at MailOnline, and also covered enterprise tech news for TechRepublic, eWEEK, and TechHQ.

Fiona cut her teeth writing human interest stories for global news outlets at the press agency SWNS. She has a Master's degree in Chemistry, an NCTJ Diploma and a cocker spaniel named Sully, who she lives with in Bristol, UK.

#6476. Asteroid Mining Will Crash the Platinum Market, But That’s Good News for Earth

Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question - what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

Platinum Group Metals, or PGMs, are absolutely critical to modern industry. Two of the most commonly used are platinum and palladium, which are critical components in everything from automotive catalytic converters (hence when thereâs a raft of people stealing them) to hydrogen fuel cells. However, these materials are exceptionally hard to come by - on Earth at least. More than 80% of the known planetary reserves are locked in deep-shaft mines located in South Africa and Russia.

Their absurd prices (tens of millions of dollars a ton) are based at least in part on how difficult they are to extract. Even at the Russian and South African mines, they are only able to glean a few grams of material per ton of rock. In the process, they require ventilation, cooling, and heavy machinery, as well as actual laborers down deep mine shafts. That sounds exactly like the kind of industry that is ripe for disruption - at least if there is another source of the raw material.

Fraser talks about whether we will mine asteroids.

Luckily, there is. Metallic (M-type) asteroids are the leftover metallic cores of protoplanets, and carry concentrations of PGMs dozens of times higher than even the richest mines on Earth. A single kilometer-wide space rock of this type holds more PGMs than humans have extracted throughout all recorded history. No wonder these particular materials have been the focus on asteroid mining efforts for decades.

AstroForge, a start-up based in California, is one of a second-round of asteroid mining start-ups that are focusing specifically on returning PGMs to Earthâs market. Instead of multi-billion dollar asteroid mining craft, they specialize in small, agile probes that cost only a few million dollars each to launch. The value of what they return, though, is much higher.

Their architecture involves latching on to the metallic asteroid using magnets. High power lasers then vaporize the asteroidâs crust, and an onboard refinery separates the PGM gas from the less valuable nickel and iron that makes up the majority of the asteroidâs bulk. After the PGMs have been refined, they are blasted back to Earth in a heat-shielded return capsule, ready to be brought to market on Earth itself. That way, the company only ships high value material rather than processing minerals that donât have as much value back down on Earth.

Isaac Arthur is much more bullish on our eventual ability to mine asteroids, as he discusses in this video. Credit - Isaac Arthur YouTube Channel

Understanding how this would affect the terrestrial market is the focus of the paper, and researchers Robert Nachtrieb and Steven Smith built a dynamic computer simulation tracking what they believe will happen to the PGM market over a 20 year period following the first successful return of a chunk of material from an asteroid. According to their model, there will be a dramatic, two-phase transition.

The first phase can be thought of as a âspace gold rushâ. The prices for PGMs have been held artificially high by lack of supply - a classic problem in traditional economics. Once the supplied amount changes - such as when new sources come online, the price begins to fall as the supply line of the classic âXâ graph moves to the right. But it doesnât happen overnight. At the start, space-based metals will be able to be sold at normal prices, allowing the asteroid mining companies to enjoy astronomical profit margins.

Those profit margins will, at least in theory, drive plenty of additional private investment, which in turn will be used to expand the production capacity of the space-based options. According to the paper, this will drive a cycle where industry profits will skyrocket to eight times what they currently are during this first phase. Thatâs enough to make whoever successfully send material back first fabulously wealthy.

But eventually, the second act will begin - what the authors describe as equilibrium collapse. Global supply of PGMs will far exceed original terrestrial amounts, and the market prices will start falling dramatically. High cost mines, such as those operating in North America, will be the first casualties. The Russian and South African behemoths, though, will not be far behind, as they will be unable to maintain a profit with the lower price caused by the increased supply. Over the course of fifteen years, terrestrial mining supplies will be completely replaced by space-mined ones, and market prices will drop by over 75%.

That might sound like terrible news for the terrestrial mining industry - and to put it bluntly, it is. But itâs great news for everyone else. Cheaper PGMs mean less expensive hydrogen electrolyzers, and therefore a less expensive transition to the âgreen economyâ for the rest of the world. In addition, space-based mining does not have all the acid mine drainage, arsenic pollution, and hazardous labor in deep tunnels that are required to get PGMs out of the ground on Earth.

Which all sounds like a much better future for humanity more generally. The problem is the engineering challenges to get to that point. Astroforge has had a few high-profile failures during its development cycle so far. But thatâs the case with any fast-moving ânew spaceâ company. It is undeniably getting closer to making this future world of green tech provided by space rocks a reality. And, if they do manage to do so, everyone involved should become extremely wealthy in a span of less than two decades.

#6475. The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's

Most planets appear to have magnetic fields, even if they're only weak, remnant fields. Earth has a strong field generated by its internal geodynamo. The other rocky planets have magnetic fields of varying strengths, with the possible exception of Venus. The outer gas planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all have strong dynamos.

But the magnetic fields generated by the ice giants Uranus and Neptune have some strange properties.

Earth's molten core and internal convection generate its magnetic fields. But the ice giants' magnetic fields are likely generated by fluids that are electrically conductive. These are water, ammonia, and methane ices under extreme pressure and temperatures that alter them and turn them into ionic and superionic phases. Not only is their electrical conductivity at play, but so is convection and the planets' rotations.

But beyond what generates them, they also have other differences. Earth's magnetic field has well-defined north and south poles that drift a little over time, and even flip every couple of hundred thousand years or so. But Voyager 2 showed us how different Uranus and Neptune are. Their fields are in disarray compared to Earth's. They're tilted and multi-peaked.

Uranus' magnetic field doesn't originate in its center, and is tilted almost 60 degrees from its axis of rotation. It's overall geometry is strange, and the magnetic field across its surface is asymmetrical in strength.

Neptune's magnetic field is similarly strange, but weaker. Like Uranus' it's tilted from its rotational axis, by about 47 degrees. It's also offset from the planet's physical center like Uranus'.

The most critical difference between the magnetic fields of Earth and those of Uranus and Neptune is that the fields around the ice giants experience shorter-term variability. In short, they're a weird mess.

While planetary scientists know that these fields are generated inside the planets, they've had to make some guesses as to why they're so strange. New research in Nature Communications Physics has made some progress understanding the pair of ice giants and their strange magnetic fields. It's titled "Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune," and the lead author is Chi Yan. Yan is a research associate at the University of Texax Jackson School of Geosciences.

"Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet," the researchers write. "These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes."

As we often say at Universe Today, understanding the oddballs and outliers in a group of objects sheds light on how processes operate across the broader group they're a part of. This is true of the ice giants and their magnetic fields. "Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars," the authors explain.

This work is based on modelled dynamos that are controlled by interior composition and temperature. They assumed that electrical conductivity increases with depth. The authors say they "produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune..."

This schematic shows the different interior layouts used in the models. a through c show radially variable electrical conductivity profiles for dynamo models with convective shell geometries. d through f show the associated shell geometry for each of a through c. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

âDeep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,â lead author Yan said in a press release. âUnder these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.â

Voyager 2 gave us our only good close-up look at Uranus and Neptune. It likely caught those fields in a snapshot in time, and the model shows both planets' magnetic fields could shift and change markedly in only decades. The fields are most likely configured much differently than when Voyager 2 visited. This is much different than on Earth, where the magnetic north pole drifts between about 5 and 60 km per year, or about one degree every few decades.

"These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow," the authors write. They explain that changes in both intensity and orientation are a possibility in the decades since Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, "though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once."

âEarthâs magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,â said Yan. âOur models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.â

This figure compares observations of Uranus' and Neptune's surface magnetic fields with the fields from models. The figure "demonstrates that the most Uranus-like snapshot from Model 6 (panel c) and the most Neptune-like snapshot from Model 11 (panel d) can change substantially on decadal timescales, with their close morphological resemblance to the respective observed fields (panels a and b) deteriorating markedly after 32 years (panels e and f)," the authors explain. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

"We demonstrate that dynamo models incorporating an electrical conductivity that increases with depth can promote non-dipolar, non-axisymmetric magnetic fields," the authors write, including the M1 peak observed at Uranus and Neptune.

The M1 peak is an important, maybe the most important part, of Voyager 2's magnetic field observations. M=1 represents the lop-sided parts of a magnetic field. On Earth and other planets like Jupiter and Saturn, the magnetic field's power is dominated by symmetric or M=0 components. So for those planets, the M-1 components are at least an order of magnitude weaker than their M-0 components.

But that's not true on Uranus and Neptune. They show a stark contrast. They both have a very strong M-1 peak, the part that represents asymmetric fields. This means that they have dipoles, quadrupoles, and octupoles that are messy and skewed from the axis of rotation.

"Despite current observational and computational limitations, our results indicate that ice-giant-like dynamos can, in some intervals, undergo substantial magnetic field variations on decadal timescales that, if confirmed by future in situ or auroral measurements, could have significant impacts on the surrounding planetary magnetospheres," the authors write.

The JWST has observed the ice giant aurorae and the charged particles involved. These particles respond to the magnetic fields, and those observations could confirm if the magnetic fields have indeed shifted since Voyager 2 visited. Researchers are still working on those observations.

The image on the left is an enhanced-color image of Neptune from NASAâs Hubble Space Telescope. On the right, that image is combined with data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. The cyan splotches are auroral activity captured with the JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Heidi Hammel (AURA), Henrik Melin (Northumbria University), Leigh Fletcher (University of Leicester), Stefanie Milam (NASA-GSFC)

âWe are busy working on whatâs contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,â said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign.

The researchers will combine the JWST data with their models and data from Voyager 2 and take their results as far as they can to try to determine the state of the magnetic fields today. But they're up against some limitations, limitations that can only be lifted by another mission to the ice giants.

There are no firm plans for a mission to the ice giants, but there are concepts. One is NASA's Uranus Orbiter & Probe that would study the planet and its moons, and even send a probe into Uranus' atmosphere. The Neptune Odyssey is another NASA concept. It would also consist of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. The science community has recognized the importance of these missions, but they're just concepts at this point.

This research may extend to the issue of habitability, though probably only tangentially. Uranus' four major moons could all potentially have subsurface oceans under icy covers, though this is far from confirmed. If they do, then Uranus' magnetic field and related radiation belts could affect these bodies of water, their longevity, and their potential habitability.

#6474. Scientists Ranked 20 Protein-Rich Foods on Health, Affordability, and Sustainability. One Surprising Food Came Out on Top

Tofu took the crown in a showdown of 20 protein-rich foods judged on health, affordability, availability, and their toll on the planet.

Protein-rich foods can look very different when cost, access, health, and environmental impact all enter the picture. In a study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, Dr. Chris Macdonald developed a framework that combines these four considerations to compare commonly consumed protein sources.

Among the 20 foods assessed, tofu took the top spot, while cheddar cheese finished last. The results followed a clear pattern: plant-based foods occupied the entire highest-scoring fifth, and animal-based products made up the lowest-scoring fifth.

Tofu’s lead came from strong results across both parts of the assessment. It earned a perfect 16 points for environmental performance, placing in the best-performing fifth for greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, land use, and freshwater use. It also scored 20 out of 24 points for health and accessibility, including full marks for providing all nine essential amino acids.

Together, these measures explain why the rankings go beyond protein content alone. They weigh the environmental costs of producing protein alongside nutritional factors and practical considerations such as price and availability.

The paper argues that ratings focused on one feature can leave consumers with an incomplete picture. A product’s performance in one area does not explain its trade-offs elsewhere. Macdonald presents the framework as a way to help people understand those competing considerations and the food systems their purchases support.

As the paper states, “Against deliberate corporate obfuscation and marketing myths, the goal of a holistic score is not to create a new label, but to foster a new literacy, one that empowers us to see the reality of the systems we are funding.

Ultimately, beyond the spreadsheets and scores, lies a fundamental reckoning: our protein choice is a referendum on the compassion we are willing to show to animals, to the planet, and to future generations.”

The research builds on Macdonald’s work at the Better Protein Institute, which examines how much protein people need for optimal health, how to shift consumer behavior effectively, and where investment could support future protein sources. By questioning common assumptions and starting from first principles, that work addresses some of the most frequently Googled questions about dietary protein.

Reference: “What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI Score” by Chris Macdonald, 1 July 2026, Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2026.1677796

#6472. Astrophysicists Want to Forecast When a Black Hole Launches Its Jets

Black holes are not just objects. Some astrophysicists prefer to call them locations. From this vantage point, they're locations where the Universe's laws of physics are pushed to their extreme limits.

Black holes are gravitational gluttons that draw everything in their vicinity towards them. When another star strays too close, the black hole can strip its gas away. The gas doesn't necessarily disappear over the event horizon and leave our observable Universe. It first gathers in a rapidly rotating accretion disk, where its temperature is raised to extreme levels. Some of this superheated material is ejected in a pair of collimated jets from the black hole's axis of rotation.

These jets are streams of plasma and particles that can reach relativistic speeds. They can have an enormous reach; the largest ones come from supermassive black holes and can extend for millions of parsecs into space. Though astrophysicists have witnessed many of these jets, their exact causes remain uncertain. The extreme gravity, magnetic fields, and temperatures around black holes is all a part of it.

Astrophysical jets shape their surroundings by heating star forming gas and moving it around on a massive scale. Stars form from cool gas, and the energy from jets works directly against that. The jets can also inflate bubbles where gas is too diffuse to collapse and form stars.

This JWST NIRCam image shows the jets coming from Messier 87, one of the most massive galaxies in the local Universe. These jets aren't from an x-ray binary, they're from its central SMBH that has billions of solar masses. It's an example of extreme astrophysical jets and an indicator of the extreme physics at black holes. Image Credit: Jan RÃ¶der, Maciek Wielgus et al., Astronomy & Astrophysics (2025)

Astrophysicists want to be able to predict when these jets are triggered so they can quickly gather follow-up observations, and new research in The Astrophysical Journal has made some progress. It's titled "Jet Forecast: Timing of Discrete Jet Ejections of Stellar-mass Black Holes Anticipated via X-Ray Properties," and the authors are Toshihiro Kawaguchi and Kazutaka Yamaoka. Kawaguchi is from the Graduate School of Science and Engineering at the University of Toyama, and Yamaoka is from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

The pair of researchers have been working on this problem for a while. In a 2025 study, they examined an x-ray binary consisting of a black hole and a donor star and found a link between the parameters of the inner accretion disk and jet activity. That research suggested that as the accretion disk's inner edge shrank towards its innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the black hole launched its jets. "This fact suggests that the jet materials originate from accreting matter from the innermost part of the disk," the authors wrote.

That was progress, but in that paper the researchers pointed out that more observations were needed. "Both X-ray spectral and timing observations are very important to understand the accretion disk states which can change very rapidly. Dense, simultaneous coverage with radio observations are also crucial to understand diskâjet interactions," the authors wrote in the conclusion to their 2025 paper.

This illustration is representative of XTE J1859+226, the system the authors studied in their 2025 paper. It shows a black hole not only drawing material away from the donor star, but also stretching the star into a distorted shape. Image Credit: J. M. Corral-Santana/Corral-Santana et al. 2011 MNRAS

Their 2025 paper was based on observations of a single black hole x-ray binary gathered during an outburst in 1999â2000. This work is based on observations of four black hole binary systems: one from the 2025 paper and three new ones.

There seem to be changes in an x-ray binary's (XRB) x-ray emissions prior to jets being launched. The spectrum is altered, and variability decreases. Astrophysicists have interpreted these changes as a signal that jets are about to be emitted. But the signals haven't been clear and reliable enough, so astrophysicists haven't been able to use them to time their follow-up observations. The researchers' previous work showed that as an accretion disk's inner edge shrank down to its ISCO, jets were launched. This could be the reliable signal astrophysicists are searching for.

This work expands their observations to more XRBs to see if this holds true. The researchers hope to develop a forecasting model for XRB jet launching so that more complete observations can be obtained.

The results show that the rapidly decreasing radius of the inner disk, called Rin, combined with a decrease in x-ray emission variability (indicated by rms), are a reliable predictor of jet launching. "All the four sources turned out to show the precursors of jet ejections (drops in Rin and rms) 1â10 days before radio activities," the authors write.

This artistâs depiction of a jet ejection shows how the jet from the black hole turns on when the inner radius of the accretion disk shrinks down to the ISCO fast enough. Image Credit: Professor Toshihiro Kawaguchi from University of Toyama, Japan and Dr. Kazutaka Yamaoka from Nagoya University, Japan.

They also found that there are no reliably detected increases in the amount of mass accreted prior to the launching of jets. "They show no huge jumps in M prior to each jet ejection," the researchers explain.

In at least one of the XRBs, that rate actually decayed in the 30 days leading up to jet launching. "We examined the time evolution of the accretion rate M of XTE J1859. It turned out to be exponentially decaying during the outburst (with an e-folding timescale of â¼30 days), and shows no huge jumps around the jet ejections," they write.

But XTE J1859 did show a tantalizing hint of enhancement. "There is a hint of â¼20% enhancement in M just before the jet productions," the authors write.

But that's just a hint, and better observations are needed to support it. "Such fine structures in the time evolution of M will be examined by the better data via the âjet forecastâ in the future," the researchers write.

Another notable finding concerns the Eddington limit. It's a theoretical threshold balanced between the inward force of gravity and the outward force of radiation. In two of the four systems, jets formed below this threshold. Some models of jet ejection say that super-Eddington accretion beyond this limit is necessary to launch jets, but these results say otherwise.

âMonitoring of Rin seems to be suitable for predicting the timing of jet ejections,â said Prof. Kawaguchi. âThe development of a âjet forecastâ would enable us to concentrate observing facilities on the expected timing of jet ejections, thereby accelerating our understanding of jet physics.â

Their jet forecasting model would be based on shrinking Rin and X-ray variability, and when both are detected, alerts would be sent out to other telescopes for more complete observations. Those observation would hopefully reveal some more of the extreme physics that dominate and define black holes.

"When both Rin and rms continuously decrease and when Rin is about to reach the ISCO, alerts can be circulated as a âjet forecastâ for triggering ToO (Target of Opportunity) observations," the authors write.

This is more than just purely academic. Earth has been subjected to bombardment by high-energy particles throughout its history. The Earth's protective magnetic shield deflects most of them, but some get through and trigger showers of secondary particles. Convincing evidence is thin, but some researchers still consider them a factor in the course of life on Earth.

âJet ejections in the Universe produce high-energy photons and particles, such as neutrinos, and such cosmic rays have long influenced the evolution of living creatures on Earth, including human beings,â concluded Prof. Kawaguchi.

#6471. Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It

Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.

Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.

Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.

“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.

Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in Cell that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.

Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.

“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”

Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence cancer patient outcomes and responses to immunotherapy. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.

The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.

Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.

The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.

Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.

Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.

“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”

The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.

“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.

Reference: “Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade” by Dipyaman Patra, Katelyn Wolfgang, Chenxian Ye, Lora Rigatti, Kelsey Ertwine, Kristin M. Morder, Jessica Jana, Ishita Baral, Drew Hurd, Kaitlin Bossong, Steven Mullett, Yingtong Dou, Stacy Gelhaus, Dario A.A. Vignali, Diwakar Davar, Anthony R. Cillo, Greg M. Delgoffe and Abigail E. Overacre-Delgoffe, 22 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055

This research received support from the National Institutes of Health (DP2AI177967, S10OD023402, S10OD032141, R35 CA263850, S10 OD032265), Damon Runyon Cancer Research Foundation, Gateway Foundation for Cancer Research (G-22-800), Cancer Research Institute Lloyd J. Old STAR Award (CRI3447), Sy Holzer Endowed Immunotherapy Fund, The Pittsburgh Foundation (MR2023-134140), National Institute of Allergy & Infectious Diseases (R01AI171483, R01AI166598), National Cancer Institute (P30CA047904, R01CA277473, P50CA121973, P50CA097190), and UPMC Hillman Cancer Center Skin Cancer and Head and Neck Cancer SPOREs.

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

In this immersive and mind-expanding book, acclaimed physicist Christophe Galfard takes you on an adventure like no other to answer the fundamental question: what is life? You’ll travel back in time to witness the cataclysmic asteroid impact that doomed the dinosaurs, experience the tumultuous forces that shaped our planet, and discover how the first stirrings of life emerged from inanimate matter.

Christophe Galfard is a theoretical physicist turned international pop-science bestselling author based in Paris. He co-authored "George's Secret Key to the Universe" with Stephen Hawking and his daughter Lucy Hawking. Galfard's most recent book, "The Universe in Your Hand: A Journey Through Space, Time, and Beyond," has been translated into over 20 languages.
